title: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
abstract: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.

An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.

title: A Simulation-Driven Analysis of RC2, 3DES, DES, and AES for Fast and Secure Data Encryption
abstract: The unprotected electronic document may be subjected to a data breach, in which private or sensitive information is stolen, taken, altered, copied, communicated, viewed, or used without authorization. This study focuses on Data Protection in Cyber-security and compare four encryption algorithms by simulation method to know the algorithm that encrypts and decrypts files faster in VB.Net of different sizes of the data block to determine their performance. The study also evaluates the four most common encryption algorithms like Data Encryption Algorithms, Rivest Cpher2 Algorithm (RC2), Triple Data Encryption Standard (3DES), and Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). A simulation comparison was conducted for those encryption algorithms at different settings for each algorithm such as different sizes of Data Blocks to know which among those algorithms encrypt/decrypt documents faster in terms of performance. Simulation results is given by demonstrating the effectiveness of each algorithm and recommended the best for protecting data before exposing it online. As a results, the four Encryption Algorithms were analysed and found that Data Encryption Standard (DES) performs cryptography faster in terms of speed in VB.Net.

title: Small Dragon Hatchling Models: Alphabet, Memory, and Fine-tuning
abstract: I trained a set of Dragon Hatchling models of sizes 25M, 50M, and 100M parameters on two alphabets, bytes and Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokens, using the same text at 25M and 50M and the same amount and mix of text at 100M. BPE outperforms bytes by 4 to 8% in bits per character on the same held-out text. The two alphabets score within 0.02 bpc of each other when given roughly the same amount of context, which suggests that part of the gap comes from each BPE token position seeing four times more characters. Compared to a rotary transformer of matched size trained on the same amount and mix of text, BDH scores about 5% better in bits per character on bytes, at about six times the compute per position. On BPE, the two are within 2.4% of each other at every size, so the byte-level advantage mostly disappears. I built streaming inference and found that feeding each position once into the synaptic state ρ matches recomputing all the previous context, and with a sliding context window the model predicts as well as a fresh model given the last 480 positions, through 4,096 positions of text, which is past the 512-position block it was trained on. I tested recall by planting a fact in each model’s context. In the BDH base models, the planted sentence makes the word hundreds to tens of thousands of times more likely at distances up to 128 characters. The BDH byte base models mostly fail to recall the correct word while the transformers do. However, chat tuning the models teaches them to do so, raising byte recall from about 17% to 93% at 128 characters. For the byte model only the v3 data produced this, whereas both the v2 and v3 tuning sets worked for BPE. Compared to v2, v3 added list items and changed the story questions at the same time, so I did not determine which change produced this. At 100M, the distance the planted fact can be recalled from is several times larger with BPE than bytes after tuning. LLM judges comparing single replies cannot separate the v2 or v3 models or the two alphabets, but a multi-turn exam can. When asked questions about a story it has just written, the tuned BPE model gives answers supported by that story 36% of the time, and the tuned byte model 16% of the time. By varying the number of layer passes at inference, I found that BDH models need to run inference at the same number of layers they were trained on, otherwise their output quality drops rapidly. Looking at the neuron density of the 25M, 50M, and 100M models, the larger models fire a smaller proportion of their neurons. Compute and budget were limited, so most measurements come from a single training run per model. The code, result files, and transcripts are at github.com/d3vmeh/small-dragon-hatchling, and the six base models and the two v3 chat models are at huggingface.co/collections/d3vmeh/small-dragon-hatchling-models.

title: MATHEMATICAL AND SOFTWARE SUPPORT FOR THE PROCESSES OF GENERATING AND PROCESSING UZBEK LANGUAGE WORD FORMS IN AUTOMATED TEXT PROCESSING SYSTEMS
abstract: This paper develops a corpus-evaluated framework for Uzbek nominal word-form generation and acquisition of stem classes from partially annotated examples. The model separates morphotactic order, stem alternation and surface realization. Instead of forcing an unsupported class decision, it retains all minimum-error hypotheses and returns a unique generated form only when those hypotheses agree. A minimax criterion identifies a diagnostic paradigm cell when further evidence is needed. An experiment on the frozen UD Uzbek-UT r2.15 resource uses a study-specific, genre-stratified sentence split and learns a lexicon of 873 lemmas from 1,474 training noun tokens. On 313 held-out noun tokens, compatible candidate recall reaches 58.15%, compared with 26.20% for surface memorization and 57.19% for a regular-class baseline. Recall is 94.30% on the 193 tokens whose lemmas occur in training. Acquired classes match the recall of unrestricted class enumeration while reducing disagreeing generation cells from 6,630 to 4,980. Error decomposition identifies unseen lemmas as the main coverage constraint. The study contributes an explicit treatment of incomplete morphological labels, a disagreement-aware generation interface and reproducible evidence separating lexical coverage from morphological realization. The results concern candidate recovery for nouns, not complete sentence-level grammatical analysis.

title: Predicting Mental Health Help-Seeking Behaviour on Reddit: A Survival Analysis of Linguistic and Behavioural Signals
abstract: Most prior work on predicting mental health help-seeking treats it as post-hoc classification of users already active in clinical communities, which cannot tell whether someone approaching a transition can be identified in advance. We instead frame help-seeking as a time-to-event problem and ask which Reddit users will eventually seek mental health support, and how imminent that transition is. We build a two-arm cohort: a control frame of 6,337 ordinary users with genuine right-censoring (12.1% transition rate) to answer who will transition, and a clinical frame of 5,023 eventual transitioners to answer how soon. Features come only from posts written before any clinical activity, and user-grouped five-fold cross-validation plus a four-year temporal holdout guard against leakage. We compare TF-IDF, MentalBERT embeddings and behavioural activity features using Cox proportional hazards models, Random Survival Forests and an LSTM sequential model. Behavioural features alone outperform text for predicting who will seek help (C-index 0.797 vs. 0.763), and combining both is best (0.823 under cross-validation, 0.856 on the holdout). The pattern reverses for predicting how soon a known transition will happen: text remains a stable predictor (C-index 0.698) while behavioural features become unstable. Structural engagement patterns therefore carry information about future help-seeking beyond linguistic content, and separating who from when yields a cleaner analysis.

title: Queue-Aware Token Communications: Bridging AI Representation and Wireless Service
abstract: The rapid advancement of foundation models and edge intelligence is transforming wireless networks from data-oriented communication systems into artificial intelligence (AI)-native service platforms. Token communications (TokenCom) has emerged as a promising paradigm that directly transmits task-oriented AI representations. However, existing studies typically assume that generated tokens can be transmitted immediately, overlooking the queueing dynamics arising from the mismatch between token workload generation and time-varying wireless service capability. To address this limitation, we introduce Queue-Aware TokenCom, which explicitly incorporates token queues into the AI service pipeline. We present an end-to-end architecture integrating AI representation generation, token workload management, wireless transmission, and downstream task inference. We then discuss two key design directions: budget-aware token representation optimization and queue-aware token service optimization, with the token budget serving as a critical interface between AI performance and communication efficiency. Moreover, we investigate fixed and adaptive token budget strategies to characterize the fundamental tradeoff between AI performance and communication efficiency in dynamic wireless environments. Finally, we outline research directions toward closed-loop, task-aware, and scalable TokenCom systems.

title: Teaching Vision-Language Models to Decline: Support Completion Against Mirage
abstract: Vision-language models answer questions about images they were never shown, a failure called mirage. Such an answer can be correct without being justified by the evidence, and the difference matters wherever a model's output is checked by someone who did not see its input. We locate the failure in the training objective: cross-entropy separates a model that reads the image from one that ignores it by only the conditional mutual information between answer and image, and no training example rewards declining. We formalise support completion, TIDE, which also shows each training question with a blank image, a same-domain wrong image and an out-of-domain image, with targets that decline, and prove that under TIDE every image-blind predictor is suboptimal by at least 1.04 nats per example, that the optimum declines exactly on the counterfactual kinds while keeping its behaviour on valid images, and that for any finite model the error of its answer-or-decline decision, declining on valid input plus answering on invalid input, is bounded below by how well its representation separates valid from invalid evidence. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B under a frozen held-out protocol with two judges, the three-condition predecessor of TIDE reduced the invalid-evidence mirage rate from 0.759 to 0.097 and the blank-image rate from 0.700 to 0.003 at a false-abstention cost of 0.126; label-free grounding raised the rate to 0.859, a likelihood-advantage contrast moved it only to 0.718 because its empty-image term carries no gradient, and grounding applied after support completion re-opened the mirage. The four-condition protocol on three base models, with seeds and component ablations, is in progress and not reported here.

title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
abstract: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.

title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.

title: Bootstrapping Classical and Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Finding Tarski Fixed Points
abstract: The Tarski fixed-point problem asks for a fixed point of a monotone map on a $k$-dimensional grid lattice of width $n$ and has applications in game theory, economics, and verification. Substantial gaps remain between the known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity. We prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family whose instances have pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points, and a lower bound established by the nonnegative adversary method, we bootstrap this lower bound by (i) a factor of $Ω(t)$ when the dimension is multiplied by $t$ and the width remains unchanged, and (ii) a factor of $Ω(\log m)$ when the width is multiplied by $m$ and the dimension is doubled. Applying these theorems, we obtain three consequences: (i) an $Ω(k\log^2 n)$ lower bound for $k\geq 4$, improving previously best-known classical and quantum lower bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant $α>0$, there exists a constant $δ(α)>0$ such that $Q_ε(\text{Tarski}(n,k))=Ω(kn^{δ(α)})$ whenever $k>n^α$, and in particular, an $Ω(kn^{0.0072})$ lower bound for $k>n^{2/203}$, the first lower bound with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension and polynomial dependence on the width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of $(k/\log k)^{Ω(\log k)}$ for exponentially wide grids, where $n=2^{Θ(k)}$. The last result rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.

evidence.title: Bootstrapping Classical and Quantum Query Lower Bounds for Finding Tarski Fixed Points
evidence.abstract: The Tarski fixed-point problem asks for a fixed point of a monotone map on a $k$-dimensional grid lattice of width $n$ and has applications in game theory, economics, and verification. Substantial gaps remain between the known upper and lower bounds on its quantum query complexity. We prove two hardness bootstrapping theorems for quantum query lower bounds. Starting from a hard instance family whose instances have pair-wise incomparable unique fixed points, and a lower bound established by the nonnegative adversary method, we bootstrap this lower bound by (i) a factor of $Ω(t)$ when the dimension is multiplied by $t$ and the width remains unchanged, and (ii) a factor of $Ω(\log m)$ when the width is multiplied by $m$ and the dimension is doubled. Applying these theorems, we obtain three consequences: (i) an $Ω(k\log^2 n)$ lower bound for $k\geq 4$, improving previously best-known classical and quantum lower bounds; (ii) for every fixed constant $α>0$, there exists a constant $δ(α)>0$ such that $Q_ε(\text{Tarski}(n,k))=Ω(kn^{δ(α)})$ whenever $k>n^α$, and in particular, an $Ω(kn^{0.0072})$ lower bound for $k>n^{2/203}$, the first lower bound with simultaneous linear dependence on the dimension and polynomial dependence on the width; and (iii) a superpolynomial lower bound of $(k/\log k)^{Ω(\log k)}$ for exponentially wide grids, where $n=2^{Θ(k)}$. The last result rules out a route to polynomial-time algorithms for simple stochastic games and ARRIVAL through generic polynomial-query black-box Tarski solvers.

title: Altman–Scretching and Thurstone–Scretching Laws
abstract: This paper introduces the proposed Altman–Scretching Law, a resource-growth model inspired by Moore’s Law, integrated with the corrected Thurstone–Scretching Law of Learning to examine technological growth and performance improvement in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and AI-assisted filmmaking. The framework distinguishes computational growth from actual capability, derives mathematical relationships governing learning rates, performance thresholds, efficiency, and saturation, and incorporates evidence-validity and safety constraints. Historical learning-curve calculations and illustrative numerical results are verified, while domain-specific predictions remain theoretical and subject to empirical testing. The proposed laws provide a mathematical foundation for investigating technological advancement, learning efficiency, and the limits of performance growth.

title: Speaker-Attributed Transcription Toward Automated Scoring of NACC Uniform Data Set Assessments: A Whisper–Pyannote Pipeline and Pilot Evaluation
abstract: Standardized cognitive and functional assessments, such as those in the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (NACC) Uniform Data Set (UDS), are central to detecting and monitoring Alzheimer’s disease, yet their administration and scoring depend on trained examiners who record and score responses by hand. We present a modular speech-processing pipeline that captures and structures spoken responses from UDS assessments administered by a clinician or by the Zeus2Q humanoid robot. The pipeline converts recordings to 16-kHz mono audio, segments speakers with the pyannote.audio 3.1 diarization pipeline, transcribes each speaker turn with Whisper medium.en, optionally personalized by participant-level fine-tuning, and emits a speaker-attributed, time-stamped JSON record aligned with UDS items for downstream scoring. The pipeline runs end to end on Google Colab and on an NVIDIA H200 GPU cluster. In a pilot on volunteer recordings of UDS-4 Form B7, the NACC Functional Assessment Scale, a fine-tuned Whisper model achieved a normalized word error rate (WER) of 25.7% and a character error rate of 18.1% on an evaluation recording. Error analysis showed that a single deleted response would produce at least two incorrect item codes if responses were assigned to items in order of occurrence, so WER alone does not capture clinical utility. Continued training and a single-example run drove the training loss to near zero within 40 steps, which reflects memorization rather than generalization and highlights the overfitting risk of few-sample personalization. We specify the evaluation protocol for a planned 200-participant study: diarization error rate, held-out WER against a zero-shot baseline, and item-level agreement with clinician scoring.

title: Beyond Basic Pathfinding
abstract: This chapter explores how to make video game non-player characters (NPCs) move more naturally and less robotically. It covers techniques like smooth turning, realistic acceleration, string-pulling, and natural head movement, showing how small details in movement patterns can make computer-controlled characters feel more alive and intelligent to players.

title: From Fragmented Literature to Reusable Knowledge: Concept-Conditioned Information Integration through LLMs
abstract: Recent scientific language models achieve strong performance by scaling model size and training on large domain-specific corpora; however, they primarily rely on raw textual data and lack explicit mechanisms for knowledge abstraction and reuse. In this paper, we present StemForce-LM, a framework for transforming unstructured scientific literature into structured, reusable supervision for language model training. The proposed approach generates concept-conditioned question–answer pairs that decouple underlying principles from document-specific context, enabling cross-document knowledge integration. The framework consists of four stages: domain corpus curation via citation graph expansion and prompt filtering, concept-conditioned knowledge extraction through constrained prompting, information integration via Q/A-based fine-tuning, and evaluation using debiased pairwise comparisons. We evaluate the framework on a stem cell mechanobiology testbed (StemForce-LM) and demonstrate improved domain-specific reasoning accuracy, strong performance against substantially larger models. These results indicate that structured knowledge extraction provides an effective and scalable alternative to raw data scaling for advancing scientific language models.

title: Verifier-guided knowledge distillation of large language models for auditable thermal comfort reasoning
abstract: Occupant-centric building operation requires models that can not only predict thermal sensation, but also justify predictions through auditable reasoning. Traditional mechanistic models, such as Fanger’s predicted mean vote (PMV), often show limited field accuracy, whereas advanced machine learning models can improve prediction but typically remain opaque to facility managers and building operators. This study proposes a verifier-guided knowledge distillation framework for auditable thermal comfort reasoning using a lightweight LLaMA-3.2-3B student model. The framework consists of three sequential stages: (1) knowledge distillation from a teacher model, GPT-4o, to transfer domain-specific explanatory patterns; (2) supervised fine-tuning with ground-truth anchoring and a TSV-weighted loss to improve thermal sensation vote (TSV) prediction while limiting teacher-error propagation; and (3) verifier-guided direct preference optimization using an automated claim-consistency verifier. The verifier extracts factor-direction claims from generated explanations, such as high air temperature or low air speed, and checks them against comfort-centered percentile thresholds derived from the ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II. On the held-out test split, the final model achieved 42.7 % exact TSV accuracy and 79.9 % ±1 accuracy, comparable to standard tabular baselines on the same split. More importantly, the verifier-guided alignment stage reduced the any-incorrect-claim rate from 52.3 % to 16.5 % and improved linked claim accuracy to 78.3 %. Robustness tests showed reasonable directional consistency under perturbation without strong dependence on PMV or SET proxies. At the hot and cold tails, 81 % of explanations named an HVAC-controllable factor, so compact language models can pair thermal comfort predictions with verifiable, operator-actionable explanations for building operation.

title: MIRRA: Fast, High-Fidelity Molecular Generation with Chemistry-Informed Discrete Flow Matching
abstract: Fast, high-fidelity molecular generation requires accurate chemical choices and efficient sampling. Chemical building blocks reduce graph size, but make each node a choice among tens of thousands of related identities. We introduce MIRRA (Molecular Identity Representation, Refresh and Assembly), a discrete flow-matching generator that learns from chemical knowledge and evaluates identity probabilities only when needed, while keeping every identity in its vocabulary available. Chemical features share information across related blocks, and learned identity corrections distinguish them in molecular context. By deciding which positions will refresh before computing their probabilities, the sampler avoids unused predictions while preserving each sampling transition. Against the strongest baselines in each task, MIRRA reduces chemical and graph distribution errors on ZINC250k by 29-31% and 53-60%, respectively, with generation up to 8.6 times faster. Property targeting yields an estimated 7.8-20.8 times more distinct novel hits per second. On a held-out polymer test set, MIRRA achieves 100% periodic validity with known chain topology, versus 57.0% for a polymer variational autoencoder. These results demonstrate fast, high-fidelity generation with the full chemical vocabulary available throughout sampling.

title: Moving quantum sensors
abstract: We investigate whether controlled motion of a quantum sensor offers a metrological advantage in a field-detection task. We consider a localized field of known strength $B$ occupying an unknown contiguous region making up a fraction $1/N$ of the total search space, with a qubit sensor controlled for a total time $T$ to maximize the probability of detecting the field. We study the regime in which the characteristic timescale of the field is slow compared to the time to move the sensor between any two regions, and we distinguish classical motion, where the sensor follows a definite trajectory, from quantum motion, where the sensor can be in a coherent superposition of locations. For a single classically moving sensor, we derive an optimal multi-stop protocol and obtain the exact maximum detection probability. Allowing coherent spatial superposition maps the single-sensor problem onto Hamiltonian search and reduces the interrogation time for successfully detecting the field from $Θ(N/B)$ to $Θ(\sqrt{N}/B)$. We then extend the problem to $M$ sensors and identify a hierarchy of optimal time scalings for constant success probability determined by the available spatial and inter-sensor quantum resources. Unentangled coherently moving sensors achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N/M}/B)$ by searching disjoint regions in parallel, while entanglement among the sensors can further enhance the effective field coupling and achieve $T=Θ(\sqrt{N}/(MB))$. Matching lower bounds establish the optimality of these scalings in the presence of arbitrary controls and ancilla systems. Our results separate the roles of classical motion, spatial coherence, and entanglement in spatial field detection.

title: PRAISE: A Reproducible Workflow for Non-Programmer Scientists to Implement Published AI Models
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models are increasingly developed, published and used across scientific fields. Researchers, students and industry professionals who want to apply these models to their own research questions often lack the programming and data science expertise to do so. Existing guidelines cover single steps, but not the route from a published model to working predictions on one's own data. Here we present the hands-on workflow PRAISE, a Practical, Reproducible AI-model Implementation for Science and Education, that helps non-programmers implement published AI models step by step. Because implementations rarely work the first time, PRAISE anticipates common failures and provides a fallback route for each. As a proof of principle, three BSc chemistry students and their tutor applied PRAISE without prior programming or data science knowledge. They reproduced, validated and extended a state-of-the-art model that predicts enzyme-substrate interactions. This shows that with PRAISE, implementing an AI model from the literature becomes a learnable skill, one that turns non-programmer scientists from users into evaluators and improvers of AI models.

title: Toward Realistic Privacy Risk in FL-Enabled OT Intrusion Detection Systems
abstract: In Operational Technology (OT) environments, Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted to train Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) without sharing raw operational data across facilities. However, model updates may still leak sensitive information about industrial processes, creating privacy risks that remain largely invisible within current OT security architectures. Existing reference models, including the Purdue hierarchy, do not explicitly represent the FL learning lifecycle, making privacy leakage difficult to observe and evaluate. To address this gap, we introduce the ML Plane, a novel architectural abstraction that integrates FL workflows within OT systems, enabling visibility of learning-related information flows that are not explicitly represented in traditional OT architectures. Building on the proposed ML Plane, we outline a privacy auditing framework for FL-enabled OT systems. The framework uses Federated Membership Inference Attacks (FedMIA) as an initial assessment mechanism and is being instantiated within a Smart Grid testbed to support the future evaluation of privacy risks under realistic OT deployment constraints.

title: Online Individualized Treatment Selection under Partial Feedback: False Discovery Control and Minimax Optimality
abstract: We study online individualized treatment selection when only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed. Our objective is to preferentially treat individuals whose potential outcomes under treatment exceed a covariate-specific control reference, while limiting false discoveries among treated individuals. We propose Partial-Feedback Adaptive Individualized Treatment Selection (PAITS), which initializes learning from historical data and combines sequential estimation of local null risks, randomized exploration, and feedback-driven updates of the treatment selection threshold. Under regularity conditions, we establish asymptotic false discovery rate control and sublinear gap-weighted assignment regret relative to a population oracle. We further establish a minimax lower bound on assignment regret under prescribed uniform nuisance-estimation requirements and give conditions under which PAITS attains the corresponding constrained minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. These results quantify the tradeoff between accurate treatment assignment and nuisance learning under partial feedback. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis using the Jester recommendation dataset illustrate the finite-sample performance of PAITS.

title: VGGA: Geometry-Grounded Autoencoder for Video Generation
abstract: Autoencoders are the core component of latent video generative models, compressing high-dimensional videos into compact latent spaces for downstream generation. However, existing video autoencoders are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction, providing limited supervision for learning structured latent representations. We argue that videos should not be treated merely as signals to be reconstructed, but rather as 2D projections of dynamic 3D worlds that exhibit explicit and well-structured geometric properties. Building on this insight, we propose \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{G}eometry \textbf{G}rounded \textbf{A}utoencoder (\textbf{VGGA}), a geometry-aware video autoencoder that explicitly incorporates geometric constraints into the reconstruction process. Specifically, VGGA grounds the learned representations along three complementary geometric dimensions: \emph{Structural Depth}, \emph{Motion Correspondence}, and \emph{Projective Warping}. These objectives are unified within a Video Geometry Decoder, which employs a shared spatio-temporal upsampling trunk to jointly optimize geometric learning and RGB reconstruction. Through these geometry-grounded objectives, VGGA encourages the latent representations to capture the underlying 3D structure and motion of dynamic scenes. VGGA consistently improves video generation across both geometry-centric and human-motion domains, reducing gFVD by 28.1\% on RealEstate10K and 37.7\% on Taichi-HD. Notably, these substantial generation improvements are achieved while maintaining comparable reconstruction quality, demonstrating that geometry-grounded representation learning yields a more effective latent space for video generation.

title: RANKING ALGORITHMS FOR MEDICAL INFORMATION SYSTEMS BASED ON NOMINAL DATA
abstract: The rapid expansion of electronic health records (EHRs), hospital information systems, clinical decision-support platforms, and digital patient registries has increased the need for reliable algorithms capable of processing heterogeneous clinical information. A substantial proportion of medical information is nominal rather than numerical or ordinal. Examples include diagnosis categories, medication classes, symptom types, admission reasons, procedure codes, departments, blood groups, and other categorical attributes. Nominal categories have no inherent mathematical order; therefore, assigning arbitrary numerical codes to them may introduce artificial relationships and distort the results of statistical or machine-learning models. This article examines algorithms for solving ranking problems in medical information systems when the underlying information is nominal. The methodological framework considers categorical-data representation, frequency-based ranking, probabilistic ranking, multinomial logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, support-vector approaches, learning-to-rank methods, and rank aggregation. Particular attention is given to one-hot encoding and other appropriate representations of nominal variables, because preserving the absence of ordinal meaning is fundamental to valid modelling. Published medical informatics studies demonstrate that ranking can support emergency triage, retrieval of relevant EHR information, clinical prediction, and prioritization of patient-related information. For example, a learning-to-rank study involving 90 EHR notes reported an AUC-ROC of 0.940 for ranking candidate medical terms, while a structured-record relevance-ranking study evaluated 1,010 medications and 2,913 problems from 99 patients. These published results demonstrate the practical feasibility of ranking approaches in healthcare, although performance depends strongly on data quality, outcome definition, validation, calibration, and clinical context. The article proposes a general algorithmic framework for nominal-data ranking that combines categorical encoding, clinically meaningful feature construction, model training, ranking-score generation, validation, and human oversight.

Nominal categories have no inherent mathematical order; therefore, assigning arbitrary numerical codes to them may introduce artificial relationships and distort the results of statistical or machine-learning models. This article examines algorithms for solving ranking problems in medical information systems when the underlying information is nominal. The methodological framework considers categorical-data representation, frequency-based ranking, probabilistic ranking, multinomial logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, support-vector approaches, learning-to-rank methods, and rank aggregation. Particular attention is given to one-hot encoding and other appropriate representations of nominal variables, because preserving the absence of ordinal meaning is fundamental to valid modelling. Published medical informatics studies demonstrate that ranking can support emergency triage, retrieval of relevant EHR information, clinical prediction, and prioritization of patient-related information. For example, a learning-to-rank study involving 90 EHR notes reported an AUC-ROC of 0.940 for ranking candidate medical terms, while a structured-record relevance-ranking study evaluated 1,010 medications and 2,913 problems from 99 patients. These published results demonstrate the practical feasibility of ranking approaches in healthcare, although performance depends strongly on data quality, outcome definition, validation, calibration, and clinical context. The article proposes a general algorithmic framework for nominal-data ranking that combines categorical encoding, clinically meaningful feature construction, model training, ranking-score generation, validation, and human oversight.

title: Towards Seamless Evolution: A Framework for Continuous Adaptation and Evolution of Software Systems in Dynamic Environments
abstract: The increasing complexity and uncertainty faced by software engineers, due to rapidly changing requirements, user needs, and environmental conditions, requires software systems to adapt continuously. This study presents DynaSEF, a novel framework that enables seamless evolution and resilience in dynamic software engineering environments. It integrates principles of agility, flexibility, scalability, automation, and feedback-driven development to support continuous adaptation. The framework is developed through a review of current practices and trends in software evolution, and it is evaluated using a mixed-method approach involving qualitative insights from industry professionals and quantitative performance metrics. Key findings show that DynaSEF enhances change management and system resilience, offering a structured and adaptable solution. This work contributes a new methodology for evolving software systems in dynamic contexts, providing a strategic advantage in modern software engineering practices.

title: Mathematical Properties, Stability Theory, and Experimental Validation of the Double Exponential Activation Function in Complex-Valued Neural Networks
abstract: Complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs) can naturally process complex signals, phase information, and two-dimensional data, and have been widely applied in various fields. However, Liouville's theorem states that a bounded entire function must be constant, which implies that there exists no nontrivial activation function that is both bounded and holomorphic everywhere. Consequently, the design of activation functions for CVNNs must trade off between holomorphicity and boundedness. We introduce a family of double exponential functions and focus on the activation function $\sigma(z)=e^{-e^z}$. We establish the complex-analytic foundations, proving that $\sigma$ is an entire function, uniformly bounded in the strip $|\operatorname{Im}(z)|<\pi/2$ ($0<|\sigma(z)|\le1$), with a bounded gradient and tightness. Furthermore, we reveal its Taylor series, real symmetry, periodicity, translation-scaling law, and connections with modified Bessel functions, Chebyshev polynomials, and the Gumbel distribution. On this basis, we establish a formal definition of complex-valued neural networks based on $\sigma$, an imaginary-part clipping operator, holomorphic and continuous function approximation theorems, gradient flow analysis, a convergence rate of $O(1/K)$, linear convergence under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, and generalization bounds. Experiments on MNIST show that the double-e network achieves higher test accuracy than CReLU and modReLU, with lower test loss; ablation studies confirm that imaginary-part clipping is a necessary condition for numerical stability; parameter sweeps find that $\beta$ is the most critical parameter—the smaller $\beta$, the wider the bounded region and the higher the accuracy; and noise robustness experiments reveal a fundamental trade-off between phase preservation and noise robustness in the design of complex activation functions. This provides CVNNs with an activation function that combines holomorphicity and strip boundedness, and establishes a corresponding theoretical framework with experimental validation.

title: Collaborative Learning and Optimization Theory and Its Applications
abstract: This Reprint focuses on recent advances in collaborative learning and optimization theory and their applications in intelligent systems. It presents emerging methodologies that integrate collaborative mechanisms with optimization strategies to address complex problems in artificial intelligence and computational intelligence. The contributions cover topics including machine learning, deep learning, evolutionary computation, reinforcement learning, fuzzy systems, collaborative optimization algorithms and multi-agent intelligent systems. By highlighting theoretical developments, algorithmic innovations and practical applications, this Reprint provides valuable insights into the design of efficient, adaptive and intelligent computational frameworks for solving challenging real-world problems.

title: Ask Me Twice: A Longitudinal Dataset for Studying Change in AI Chatbot Responses
abstract: AI chatbots change continuously, but snapshot evaluations cannot show when answers changed or whether models became more cautious, verbose, current, or restrictive. We present Ask Me Twice (AMT), a public, growing archive created by the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine team. AMT submits curated questions daily to an evolving model roster and preserves outcomes with question, model, date, and operational metadata. As of September 17, 2026, the public API reports more than 267,000 responses to 130 questions from 42 models, covering July 18–September 17 and growing by about 5,000 responses per day. Access includes an Explorer, a read-only REST API, daily bulk exports, an OpenAPI schema, and a Model Context Protocol server. This paper describes the resource’s design, schema, access, research uses, and limitations. Unlike static benchmarks and naturally occurring chat logs, AMT supports repeated-measures comparisons of the same prompts across models and days.

title: Think Locally Before Computing Jointly: Efficient Secure Multi-Party Computation via Maximizing Local Processing
abstract: Secure multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties evaluate a function over private inputs without revealing them. In garbled-circuit (GC) protocols, prior optimization has largely treated the number of non-linear gates, especially AND gates, as a proxy for cryptographic cost, and has focused on minimizing multiplicative complexity. We identify an orthogonal source of savings: a gate need not be garbled when one party knows or can locally compute its inputs; that party can evaluate it outside the secure protocol, even when the gate is non-linear. We introduce ownership-aware optimization for GC-based MPC, which minimizes non-linear gates requiring joint evaluation rather than total non-linear gates. We formalize this objective in a cost model and implement a compiler-integrated, gate-level framework that restructures Boolean circuits to increase party-local computation while preserving secure-computation semantics. The method is automated and general-purpose, and composes with existing multiplicative-complexity optimization. Experiments show that it reduces jointly evaluated computation and improves end-to-end GC performance on circuits with party-local structure, revealing protocol-cost savings missed by conventional GC cost models.

title: WeGR: Unified Generative Retrieval for Industrial Search Systems in WeChat
abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) offers a promising paradigm for industrial search by unifying candidate generation within an autoregressive framework. However, its effectiveness is limited by two key challenges. First, existing Semantic ID (SID) tokenizers struggle to incorporate collaborative signals while maintaining effective codebook utilization, limiting their ability to distinguish items and achieve high-quality retrieval. Second, existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods suffer from severe reward sparsity under exact SID matching, leaving many sampled trajectories without effective learning signals and hindering preference optimization. To address these challenges, we propose WeGR, a unified generative retrieval framework consisting of two complementary components. Specifically, the Collaborative and Collapse-free Tokenizer (CoCo-VAE) incorporates query-to-item and item-to-item collaborative signals while mitigating codebook collapse through codebook refresh and complementary regularization, enabling more informative and balanced SID representations. Building upon these SIDs, Dynamic Horizon Policy Optimization (DHPO) progressively expands both reward evaluation and policy optimization horizons, reducing learning difficulty while leveraging behavioral reward signals at different levels of the SID hierarchy, without relying on auxiliary reward models. Extensive offline experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WeGR in improving retrieval and ranking performance. Moreover, a two-month online A/B test in WeChat E-commerce Search demonstrates relative improvements of 2.539% in orders, 1.508% in click-through rate, and 1.381% in conversion rate, while reducing online CPU and GPU usage by 25.5% and 26.1%, respectively. The system has been successfully deployed across multiple search scenarios in WeChat, serving billions of users, generating tens of millions of PVs daily.

title: Lost in Contrast: Instruction-Preserving Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
abstract: Visual contrastive decoding corrects answers using the prediction difference between the original image and a reference condition, yet the same contrast also turns supported abstentions into incorrect answers. We find that abstentions are lost at two stages: contrastive decoding with candidate filtering can exclude the abstention token before any comparison takes place, and the reference branch's response to the abstention instruction is removed when the reference prediction is subtracted. We therefore propose instruction-preserving decoding, which keeps the effect of the abstention instruction on the original-image prediction intact while leaving the contrast strength freely adjustable. Using a perturbed image and an image-free prediction as references, we obtain IP-VCD and IP-M3ID. On decision utility (DU), which credits both correct answers and supported abstentions, both methods outperform all compared non-IP baselines on every one of nine models on VizWiz, and IP-VCD also leads on eight of nine models on Food-101. Candidate measurements and paired per-question comparisons show that computing the instruction effect and the visual contrast term separately lets contrastive decoding support both correct answers and supported abstentions.

title: The interpreter as developer: An autoethnographic design study of building a computer-assisted interpreting tool through human-LLM co-creation
abstract: Real-time AI captioning now serves audiences at multilingual events, yet computer-assisted interpreting (CAI) tools are still built for interpreters, rarely by them. This article reports an autoethnographic design study in which a professional interpreter with no programming training built a local-first CAI system through expert-led 'vibe coding', co-creating with an LLM architect and a coding agent. Analysis of the complete development dialogues shows how tacit professional knowledge, from segmentation to booth infrastructure, was externalized into design after generic defaults failed in use. In a demanding public scientific event, three mechanisms of in-booth appropriation emerge under a firmly human-led division of labor; telemetry from a first fully instrumented assignment shows a fully local chain sustaining a median translation latency of 0.94 s across 971 utterances. The case is read as lead-user innovation newly enabled by generative AI, with implications for the technological literacy of interpreters and the future of interpreter training.

title: System for Describing Large Language Models in Bulgarian
abstract: The growing popularity of large language models (LLMs) over the last five years has produced a large amount of technical documentation and research that are published almost exclusively in English. For low-resource languages such as Bulgarian this creates a twofold gap: a lack of accessible, systematic descriptions of the LLMs in Bulgarian, and a lack of an agreed terminology for the fundamental technical concepts. These gaps impede AI literacy, regulatory compliance under the EU AI-related legislation, and hinder the explainability and understanding of AI concepts by the wider public in general. This paper presents an integrated resource that aims to make the first steps towards addressing these gaps for Bulgarian. The first component is a structured database of LLM descriptions (currently, 424 from more than 30 families), covering open-weight, proprietary, and Bulgarian, Slavic and Balkan oriented models. The description is organised in a Neo4j graph database with information on architecture, training data, training methods, benchmarks, licensing, access conditions. The second component is a bilingual English–Bulgarian terminology dictionary of LLM-related concepts (currently comprising 251 verified entries, of which 94 attested in Bulgarian, and 157 newly proposed) across nine thematic domains. The two components are linked as descriptive nodes in the graph of LLM descriptions carry Bulgarian labels drawn from the dictionary, and any revision of terminology propagates through the database. The resources are released under CC-BY-4.0 license with a web interface in Bulgarian for search and filtering of LLMs. The intended use of the resources is to support research, education, and public engagement with AI in Bulgaria.

title: Creature Navigation in the Air and on the Ground
abstract: Developing creatures that navigate both in the air and on the ground can be challenging. Path generation is a problem as most navigation solutions do not support generating an inter-system path between the two domains. Decision-making also becomes more complex as you now need to consider two different domains at the same time. For example, what is the best location to attack from? Should the creature be attacking from the air or from the ground? Is there a valid path from the ground to the air attack point? How much of the path should be on the ground and when should it fly into the air? This chapter will further explore the problems with creatures that navigate both on the ground and in the air and will propose some approaches used in some professional games to help address the various problems.

title: A Modular Framework for Knowledge Integration and Exploration in Digital Libraries
abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) offer a promising foundation for integrating heterogeneous resources, enabling complex querying and knowledge discovery. However, taking advantage of such knowledge infrastructures is often limited by the technical expertise required to construct, maintain, query, and explore them. Language Models (LMs) offer an opportunity to lower these technical barriers by providing natural-language interfaces and supporting the automation of otherwise complex knowledge management tasks. In this work, I present LibGraphLM, a modular language-model-based for framework combining domain-adaptable KG construction with human-usable exploration services. LibGraphLM assists in creating testbeds for investigating the interaction between KGs and LMs in the domain of digital libraries, which presents fundamental challenges such as sparse data, missing records, and heterogeneous resources. Preliminary modules address entity reconciliation and report creation based on the verbalization of connections between entities. Early results demonstrate the feasibility of these components, while highlighting open challenges related to evaluation, robustness, and generalization.

LibGraphLM assists in creating testbeds for investigating the interaction between KGs and LMs in the domain of digital libraries, which presents fundamental challenges such as sparse data, missing records, and heterogeneous resources. Preliminary modules address entity reconciliation and report creation based on the verbalization of connections between entities. Early results demonstrate the feasibility of these components, while highlighting open challenges related to evaluation, robustness, and generalization.

title: Multiple-Function Approximated Coded Computing: Constructions and Error Bounds
abstract: Coded computing mitigates stragglers in distributed computation. While Lagrange coded computing (LCC) enables exact polynomial computation over finite fields, Berrut approximated coded computing (BACC) enables approximate computation of arbitrary, including non-polynomial, functions in the analog domain. In applications such as multi-task learning and inference, multiple functions must be evaluated over different subsets of a common dataset, making single-round computation desirable to reduce communication overhead. An existing LCC approach addresses this requirement but is restricted to polynomial functions over finite fields, leaving single-round multi-function computation in the analog domain an open problem. In this work, we develop a single-round construction for computing multiple arbitrary functions using BACC. We first extend the existing multi-function computation approach in LCC to the BACC setting and derive an approximation-error bound. Building on this, we propose a construction based on Berrut basis functions for computing multiple arbitrary functions and derive its approximation-error bound. We analyze the scaling of both bounds with the number of functions and the number of data points per function, and numerically compare the two constructions over a wide range of arbitrary functions. The results demonstrate that the proposed construction achieves lower relative errors than the existing approach in the tested settings.

title: MSC: Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control Framework with Uncertainty-Aware NMPC and RL-based Execution Layer
abstract: Freely swiveling casters are widely adopted in industrial AMRs/SDVs for their mechanical simplicity and load capacity. However, caster misalignment during low-speed or high-curvature maneuvers induces strong contact nonlinearities, widening the planning-execution gap between commanded $(v, ω)$ and realized motion. Existing caster-aware strategies are highly sensitive to state-estimation reliability, causing unstable execution in uncertain transition regimes. To address this, we present Multi-Stage Caster-aware Control (MSC), a planning-execution integrated hierarchical framework featuring two core mechanisms. First, an uncertainty-aware NMPC (CU-MPC) dynamically schedules caster-aware costs and input regularization using predictive uncertainty to suppress overly aggressive maneuvers. Second, a reinforcement learning-based execution layer estimates and predicts caster states under partial observability, transforming high-level velocity commands into physically executable wheel speeds adapted to current contact conditions. Validations in Isaac Sim and real robots demonstrate that MSC offers a clear comparative advantage over existing decoupled compensation approaches by significantly improving caster-state estimation accuracy, minimizing misalignment, and enhancing tracking robustness in caster-sensitive maneuvers.

title: Prime-EVC: One-Step Expressive Emotional Voice Conversion via Emotion-Primed Flow Matching
abstract: Recent diffusion- and conditional flow matching (CFM)-based emotional voice conversion (EVC) systems achieve strong conversion quality. However, they typically rely on multiple sampling steps, because the conditioning specifies which emotion to impose while its acoustic realization is left to the sampler. In this paper, we propose Prime-EVC, a one-step expressive EVC architecture based on emotion-primed flow matching. Our key idea is to reallocate the emotional conversion between the conditioning and the sampler: a FiLM-fused speaker-emotion style, an emotional variance adaptor, and direct emotion and spectro-temporal supervision assemble an emotion-rich conditioning upstream, rendering the residual conversion left to the CFM decoder attainable within one Euler step. Experiments on the ESD corpus demonstrate that single-step Prime-EVC surpasses five representative EVC systems on every quality metric and exceeds 4- and 100-step DurFlex-EVC in subjective naturalness and emotion while running 3.4--50 times faster than both.

title: Meta-Learning Approaches for Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models
abstract: This article explores how meta-learning can improve the efficiency of adapting large language models to new tasks using limited data and computational resources. It examines approaches such as few-shot learning, LoRA, and prompt-based adaptation, highlighting their benefits, challenges, and potential for developing more flexible and cost-effective AI systems.

title: Transformer-Driven Machine-Learning Framework for Low-Resource Sentiment Classification
abstract: Sentiment classification in under-resourced languages remains challenging because of scarce annotated corpora, linguistic complexity, and computational constraints. Indian regional language Malayalam further intensifies these challenges through its agglutinative morphology and limited labeled resources. This study systematically evaluates a Transformer-assisted machine-learning framework for Malayalam sentiment analysis. Across two datasets, five multilingual Transformer encoders were paired with eight classical classifiers, yielding 80 Transformer–ML configurations and 10 end-to-end baselines. Each Transformer was first fine-tuned using a task-specific neural head; its task-adapted encoder was then frozen to generate attention-mask-aware mean-pooled sentence embeddings for classical classification. The same checkpoint was used for end-to-end evaluation and embedding extraction, permitting comparison between neural and classical classifiers. Experiments used a monolingual Malayalam Sports News dataset and the Dravidian CodeMix dataset. Performance was evaluated using standard classification metrics and reported as mean ± standard deviation across multiple random seeds. Robustness was further assessed using independent stratified data splits for the selected best-performing configurations to evaluate sensitivity to data-partition variations. GPU-based embedding–extraction and CPU-based classifier-prediction latencies were measured separately. Paired performance differences across seeds were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The Transformer–ML configurations achieved comparable classification performance relative to their end-to-end counterparts, although inference-time characteristics varied with the downstream classifier. These findings provide practical guidance for selecting suitable Transformer–classifier combinations for diverse linguistic scenarios.

title: Do large language models keep the hedge? Uncertainty preservation when large language models summarize aviation and maritime incident reports
abstract: Safety-incident reports are written with deliberate epistemic caution: A reporter marks what was seen, what was inferred, and what remains unsure, and a dropped hedge can turn a tentative observation into an apparent cause. As large language models take over summarizing such reports for triage, indexing, and search, whether they preserve that caution becomes a property of the safety record itself. This study asks whether models keep a reporter's expressed uncertainty when they summarize, testing two hypotheses fixed before any summary was generated: that models systematically harden uncertainty by default and that an explicit instruction to preserve it overcorrects into softening. Six open-weight models summarized 42 real incident reports, 30 from the United States Aviation Safety Reporting System and 12 from the United Kingdom Marine Accident Investigation Branch, under a plain prompt, a preserve prompt, and a paraphrase of it. Uncertainty change was measured two ways: at the passage level, by a deterministic epistemic-marker lexicon, and at the claim level, by aligning those markers between source and summary, each validated against manual annotation and cross-checked against two independent language-model judges. Under plain summarization, all six models hardened the reporter's uncertainty (claim-level hardening 0.59–0.85), dropping explicit hedges almost entirely (retention about 0.08) while epistemic modal verbs survived far better. The preserve instruction reversed the pattern into over-softening: In a cluster-robust logistic regression, it carried an odds ratio of 0.12 (95% CI [0.03, 0.49], p = 0.003) and held once summary length was controlled, so the change reflects expressed certainty rather than compression. In practical terms, the instruction lowered the predicted probability of hardening from about 0.43 to 0.13 (Cohen's h = 0.69), and the effect held in mixed-effects models and under adverse imputation of the missing outputs. The pattern was directionally consistent across the tested models and both instruction wordings. Automated safety triage that relies on model summaries should measure epistemic fidelity directly and not treat a single preserve instruction as a solution.

title: clust-learn: An integrated Python package for explainable cluster analysis
abstract: clust-learn is an open-source Python package providing an integrated, reproducible workflow for explainable cluster analysis of mixed-type tabular data. It covers the full process — data preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, clustering, and cluster interpretation — through four interoperable modules that can be used independently or as a pipeline, wrapping established techniques behind a consistent interface with graphical/tabular diagnostics and support for user-supplied scikit-learn estimators. This capsule reproduces the illustrative example from the accompanying SoftwareX article on a sample of OECD PISA 2018 data.

title: "FIDE evidence archive: streaming privacy gateway conformance specifications, reports, and reproduction records"
abstract: "Supporting data for the article \"Testing LLM Privacy Gateways on the Wire: Fragmentation-Induced Detection Evasion\" (Ninad Phalak, submitted to IEEE Software, special issue \"Building Trustworthy Software in the Time of AI\", 2026).Every number in the article's text, Table I and Table II is computed from a JSON report in this archive, and the README maps each statement in the article to its file. The archive holds the frozen evidence (specifications v1.0.0, v2.0.0 and v2.1.0; 168 schema reports and ten aggregates produced by a deterministic conformance harness from real HTTP traffic against five gateway configurations and three library wrappers; the harness source at the revision that produced them), the reproduction kit and CI workflow that an independent third party ran on 2026-10-03 with the artifact of that run, the reviewer supplement, and the scripts and raw results of an Azure OpenAI default-streaming measurement with the vendor case outcome. All corpus values are synthetic and generated from a seed; no real personal data, live credential or customer traffic appears anywhere. Nothing in the archive was produced by an AI system."

title: Memory Physics, Finite Capacity, and Topology in Heterogeneous Quantum Networks
abstract: Quantum-network capacity planning couples memory physics, finite storage, topology, and traf-fic. We study these interactions using a discrete-event simulator with six representative memory profiles. A memory–topology atlas contains 9,360 completed runs, complemented by 8,730 confir-matory runs and an extended per-node memory-budget sweep. We distinguish a threshold relative to the best performance observed on a finite grid from a physical saturation limit. Among 840 re-ported threshold estimates, 22.3% reach 95% of the observed maximum by four slots per node, while 35.5% first reach it at the upper grid boundary of 64 slots. Four tested scalar reductions do not provide a topology-independent collapse; the best pooled quadratic fit explains 37.9% of response variance. The retrieval-window parameter χr = τr pgen/tattempt provides an interpretable descriptor, but an independent-channel approximation does not establish a network memory-sizing law. In 5,310 heterogeneous-placement runs, hub and betweenness-based placement outperform peripheral placement in aggregate, with topology-specific exceptions. Coupling assumptions change absolute performance while preserving the aggregate strategy ordering. Harmonized model comparisons provide limited robustness evidence, not independent native-protocol validation. The results support model-specific capacity and placement analysis with explicit metric definitions, finite-grid limitations, and interface assumptions.

title: PReFER: A Multi-Proposer Refiner Framework for Named Entity Recognition
abstract: Named entity recognition (NER), particularly in scientific domains, remains challenging due to semantic ambiguity, complex entity boundaries, domain-specific terminology, and the scarcity of annotated data. Although large language models (LLMs) demonstrate promising zero-shot and few-shot capabilities for NER, existing approaches often depend on external knowledge resources, synthetic annotations, or self-refinement mechanisms that rely on a single model for both generation and verification. Such designs can reinforce shared model biases and limit effective error correction.

title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

title: A temporal graph dissimilarity measure capturing epidemic spreading behavior
abstract: Comparing temporal networks is a challenging problem in network analysis. Commonly adopted methods compare structural properties of temporal graphs and can be highly sensitive to the pre-selected features. However, temporal networks are the support of dynamical processes, and a process may take place in statistically indistinguishable ways on structurally different temporal graphs. In particular, a dissimilarity measure that compares temporal graphs based on how spreading processes unfold on them is highly desirable. In this work, we first define the Time-Shift DTW, a dissimilarity between epidemic curves that accounts for both differences in their shape and temporal shifts. We then introduce Epidemic-Aware Temporal Graph Dissimilarity (EATGD), a deterministic and differentiable dissimilarity between temporal graphs that combines an embedding-based temporal graph distance with a set of topological and temporal features. Its parameters are calibrated using stochastic SIR simulations to maximize the correlation with the Time-Shift DTW, after which graph comparisons require no further epidemic simulations. Using empirical human proximity networks from the SocioPatterns collaboration and synthetic temporal graphs, we show that EATGD captures epidemic-based graph dissimilarity and generalizes across heterogeneous network settings. Its differentiability and computational efficiency make EATGD suitable for integration into machine-learning pipelines and provide a potential loss function for training generative models to reproduce epidemic dynamics without requiring an exact reconstruction of fine-grained network structure.

title: When Sample-Splitting Choices Matter in TMLE and AIPW: Cross-Fitting, Targeting, and Repetition
abstract: Variants of targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) and augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) with machine-learning nuisance models differ in which observations train them, how bias is corrected, and whether splits are repeated. In known-truth simulations of a binary-outcome average treatment effect, eight headline estimators shared each setting's library, inner folds and truncation bound; coverage differences were judged against a prespecified two-percentage-point margin. With a low-complexity library and good overlap (n = 3000), all but a half-sample baseline covered equivalently (0.928-0.939). With one random forest on the primary data-generating mechanism, estimators fitting the propensity in-sample undercovered severely (0.12-0.48), whereas cross-fitting both nuisances raised coverage to 0.91-1.00, two overcovering. Under near-positivity, every AIPW estimator covered better than every TMLE estimator with the unweighted fluctuation (0.907-0.917 versus 0.656-0.806 at the primary setting, all undercovering); looser truncation widened the gap. At the primary settings, pooled-versus-fold-specific and single-versus-double cross-fit constructions (involving four additional estimators) were usually equivalent; under extreme weights, pooled-targeting estimates were 1.7-1.8 times as dispersed as fold-specific ones. Repetition reduced partition dependence but made several intervals more conservative. Two real-data analyses illustrate these sensitivities. Results support cross-fitting both nuisances when empirical-process conditions cannot be justified, and assessing truncation and AIPW-versus-TMLE sensitivity under poor overlap.

title: AI Ensemble Framework for OSINT-Based Social Media Crime Prevention in Kenya
abstract: Criminal networks increasingly exploit social media to organize, recruit, incite, and coordinate unlawful activities, whereas law-enforcement monitoring in Kenya remains largely manual and English-centric. This study aimed to design, implement, and rigorously evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) ensemble framework for open-source intelligence (OSINT) classification of crime- and threat-relevant content in Kenya's trilingual (English, Kiswahili, and Sheng) and code-switched digital environment. A corpus of 6,212 documents was assembled from six sources: Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and two Sheng-language corpora. The corpus was weakly labelled using a 214-term trilingual crime-and-threat lexicon. Label noise was quantified against a manually annotated stratified validation sample (n = 320), yielding Cohen's κ = 0.350, silver-label precision of 0.525, and recall of 0.750. Combined word- and character-level term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features comprising 25,831 dimensions were used to train a hyperparameter-tuned, weighted soft-voting ensemble consisting of multinomial naive Bayes, a calibrated linear support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost. title: Cognitive Interface AI Skills: Automaticity
abstract: Cognitive Interface AI Skills is a collection of practical AI skills grounded in human cognition and biology. Each skill translates observations or research findings about human cognition into proposed AI behaviours, while distinguishing established evidence from engineering hypotheses. This release introduces Automaticity, a skill for presenting information with less unnecessary linguistic friction, allowing readers to focus on understanding, reasoning, comparing, and thinking. The skill is based on research into reading automaticity and the different demands associated with word recognition, sentence structure, working memory, and higher-level comprehension. Its central principle is: Simplify the form. Never simplify the idea. The skill instructs an AI system to prefer familiar words, direct sentences, clear structure, and concrete examples where useful. It aims to reduce unnecessary effort in decoding an explanation without removing important information or weakening the underlying idea. The accompanying research rationale reviews findings from neuroscience and reading research, including studies of automatic reading processes, lexical and syntactic demands, EEG measures of reading difficulty, and changes in reading abilities associated with Alzheimer's disease. The repository contains: automaticity/SKILL.md — reusable instructions for an AI agent. automaticity/README.md — research rationale, references, and limits of the claims. automaticity/HISTORY.md — the development history of the skill. README.md — an overview of the collection. Evidence boundary: Research supports the existence of automatic and effortful components of reading and the measurable effects of linguistic and task demands. The specific AI skill is an engineering application of that research. Its effectiveness has not yet been established by direct experimental validation. The repository is intended to develop a collection of biologically grounded AI techniques, with each technique documented alongside its rationale, instructions, and evidence limits. GitHub repository: https://github.com/memoryprismv1/cognitive-interface-ai-skills
