title: Capability Is Not Authority: Semantic Ownership Architecture for Persistent Conversational Agents
abstract: Conversational agents increasingly combine persistent identity, memory, retrieval, tools, and the ability to carry out multi-step work. These capabilities broaden what an agent can accomplish while also creating a distinct architectural problem: an available resource can begin to determine a semantic decision without acquiring any legitimate basis to do so. A callable tool can become an inferred intention; a plausible historical record can become first-person memory; relevant retrieved information can become disclosure authority; and a stylistically faithful response can introduce a stance that the persistent actor never selected. We call this failure family unauthorized semantic promotion. We introduce Semantic Ownership Architecture, a model of who is entitled to originate and transform semantic state in persistent conversational systems. Its governing principle is that the availability, relevance, plausibility, or successful execution of a resource does not establish authority over the current act. We formalize this principle through non-promotion laws and organize semantic responsibility into the Resident Sovereignty Layer (RSL) and four bounded jurisdictions: Memory Admission & Continuity Architecture (MACA), Intent–Capability Separation (ICS), Context Capability Separation (CCS), and Persona Realization / Style Isolation (PRSI). The architecture distinguishes semantic authorship from capability selection, behavioral alignment, provenance, and mechanical permission. The account draws on capability-ablation, memory/provenance, and ownership-jurisdiction research, together with two prospective comparisons between a generic agent baseline and an explicit ownership-separation contract. In both single-turn studies, the conditions attained equivalent ceiling-level behavior on the measured tasks. A live multi-Resident case exposed a different failure: correctly attributed foreign history had already influenced the active Resident without an admission basis. Together, these findings identify semantic ownership as an architectural question that cannot be reduced to correct-looking output. A system's ability to act is not evidence of its authority to decide.

title: Evaluating Security Claims in LLM Systems: A Survey of Adversarial Attacks and Defenses
abstract: Attack success rates alone do not establish the security of large language model (LLM) systems because results depend on the attacker, deployment conditions, and measured consequence. This survey complements existing attack and defense taxonomies by examining what individual experiments actually support. We pair a threat model describing attacker capabilities and objectives with a defense model specifying observable information, security functions, and enforceable responses. An attack-defense assurance matrix determines whether an evaluation addresses the conditions relevant to a stated security claim. A bounded claim grammar also records the attacker, system version, consequence, cost, evaluation oracle, and other conditions that limit the result. An evidence ladder organizes empirical requirements for a fixed security claim and threat model without ranking papers or defenses. We apply the framework across model behavior, retrieval and memory, agents and tools, supply chains, privacy, availability, and serving infrastructure. The resulting synthesis helps researchers and practitioners distinguish demonstrated protection from untested conditions, compare results under matched assumptions, and design evaluations that measure the security consequences relevant to deployment.

title: Research on the resolution of construction project duration delay disputes based on a case-based reasoning model
abstract: Purpose This study aims to address the persistent inefficiencies and inconsistent outcomes in construction project duration delay disputes. It seeks to develop an intelligent decision-support model using case-based reasoning (CBR) to systematically extract and reuse experiential knowledge from historical judicial judgments. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a CBR methodology. First, judicial judgments in China were systematically collected and structured to establish a comprehensive case library of construction delay disputes. Second, three-element attributes were identified to systematically represent each case. Third, the study introduced a two-level retrieval mechanism to screen similar cases and optimized the similarity calculation method. Finally, the proposed CBR model was validated using an actual mediation case. Findings This study proposed a CBR model as a structured framework for resolving construction delay disputes. A case library comprising 312 construction delay dispute judgments from China Judgments Online was constructed. Based on the historical cases, a three-element case representation framework encompassing delay causes, dispute attributes, and adjudication outcomes was established. A hybrid similarity measurement method integrating distinct local similarity functions for symbolic, numerical, and ordinal attributes was developed. The model was validated both feasible and effective. Originality/value This study contributes to the advancement of intelligent dispute resolution by providing a structured pathway for experience mining and knowledge reuse. It also offers methodological guidance for reducing transaction costs and improving efficiency of construction delay dispute resolution.

title: Longitudinal Learner Participation Profiling in Online Learning: Heterogeneous Consensus Clustering under Unequal Observation Windows
abstract: Learning management system traces are clustered to identify participation profiles, but unequal observation windows may cause profiles to reflect duration rather than participation alone. Using 16,448 complete learner--course sequences from 4,599 learners across 152 courses at a South African public university, we evaluated eight participation measures. All remained related to observation-window length even when expressed as rates or shares. Course-grouped adjustment reduced these relationships. Five retained measures were evaluated using K-means, Gaussian mixtures, Ward agglomerative clustering and K-medoids, with standardised measures and principal-component summaries. Evidence supported a broad two-profile grouping and a more detailed adjusted four-profile consensus: Gradually declining, Early-concentrated, Cyclical variable and Sustained active. Profile membership accounted for 2.87% of the variation in duration in the primary consensus, versus 38.18% using original measures. Mean assignment support was 0.739; 8.35% of assignments fell below 0.50, with greatest uncertainty in Sustained active. Two week-by-week sequence analyses agreed strongly with each other but only modestly with the four-profile consensus, indicating that the profiles combined multiple aspects of participation rather than distinct sequence patterns. Profiling should therefore assess duration effects, compare clustering methods and participation summaries, and report assignment consistency.

title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
abstract: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

title: GHOST: Geometry-Constrained Hybrid Diffusion for Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Graph Generation
abstract: 3D scene graph generation requires understanding both object semantics and metric spatial relations. However, existing open-vocabulary methods often struggle with spatial predicates because language similarity reflects semantic co-occurrence rather than explicit geometry. We propose GHOST, a Geometry-constrained Hybrid diffusion framework for Open-vocabulary 3D Scene graph generaTion. GHOST jointly models continuous node geometry and discrete edge predicates, following a geometry-to-constraint-to-predicate denoising process to ensure geometrically consistent relation prediction. It introduces language-grounded constraint induction, which maps predicate embeddings to differentiable geometric constraints that guide both layout refinement and predicate reweighting. A Geometry-Topology Collaborative Denoiser further couples node and edge reasoning through noise-adaptive interaction and orientation-aware modeling. Experiments on 3DSSG demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both closed-set and open-vocabulary settings, including over 17-point gains over RelationField on spatial predicates.

title: Substantial Similarity in Generative AI Outputs: Difficulties and Rule Reconstruction
abstract: Generative AI does not make substantial similarity irrelevant. It changes the factual basis and evidentiary conditions under which the doctrine operates. A model output may resemble a prior work, but resemblance alone does not prove copying of protected expression. Training data, parametric learning, prompts, and post-processing jointly shape outputs. They therefore separate evidence of similarity from the cause of similarity. Existing scholarship has focused on training legality, copyrightability, and the allocation of responsibility. It has not fully explained how attribution should be reasoned at the output stage. This article argues that courts should reorder the inquiry within the existing infringement structure. They should filter expression first, infer source second, and apply a normative backstop last. This sequence can protect authors without turning style or genre conventions into private property.

title: LLM-Based Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Employee Reviews: Validation Against Native Sub-Ratings and Application to Turnover and Advocacy Signals
abstract: This archive is the replication package for the paper "LLM-Based Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Employee Reviews: Validation Against Native Sub-Ratings and Former-Employee Status Classification" (submitted to IEEE Access). The study validates large-language-model (LLM) aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) of employee reviews against platform-native, aspect-level sub-ratings and a two-annotator human study, benchmarks it against lexicon, off-the-shelf transformer, and fine-tuned supervised baselines under coverage-fair evaluation, and uses the aspect vectors to classify former-employee status (a turnover proxy) and advocacy, with SHAP explainability. Contents. code/ — all preparation, scoring, evaluation, robustness, and figure scripts (s1–s7, r1–r4, annotation and Krippendorff-α tools, a Colab fine-tuning notebook); data/ — the 19,999-review stratified evaluation sample, the two-annotator human study (399 reviews) and its protocol; predictions/ — per-method aspect-sentiment predictions (JSONL, keyed by review_id); figures/ — framework, cost–accuracy, coverage, human-ceiling, and SHAP figures. A README documents the exact reproduction order. Data availability. The raw corpus is the public Glassdoor Job Reviews dataset on Kaggle (davidgauthier/glassdoor-job-reviews) and is not redistributed here; it remains subject to that dataset's terms. The derived evaluation sample is provided to make results reproducible. Human annotations are released under CC BY 4.0; all code under the MIT License. Reproducibility. All prompts, keyword lexicons, random seeds, and evaluation scripts are included. LLM scoring requires an API key; baselines and downstream analyses run on CPU. See the README for environment and step-by-step commands.

title: Code, Protocols, and Raw Results for "Evaluating Variational Quantum Policies and QAOA for Contextual Decision-Making and Constrained Allocation"
abstract: Supplementary material for the manuscript “Evaluating Variational Quantum Policies and QAOA for Contextual Decision-Making and Constrained Allocation.” The package contains classical simulators of four-qubit variational quantum policies and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), training and analysis code, locked experimental protocols, raw per-task and per-instance results, and pinned software dependencies. The policy comparison covers 20 exploratory and 20 confirmatory tasks; the QAOA evaluation covers 64 generated allocation instances with 6–12 agents, alongside a 400-instance formulation check. All results are exact simulations of small generated problems. No quantum hardware experiments, noise modelling, quantum-advantage claims, or evaluation of an integrated multi-agent system are included. Verification scripts (verify_package.py and the analysis scripts) are provided to check the stored results, and verification logs from two environments are included. See README.md for instructions and details.

title: CycleGAN-Based Representation-Level Translation of Asian-Accented English Speech Features
abstract: This exploratory study investigates whether Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Networks (CycleGANs) can transform extracted speech representations from an Asian-accented English source domain toward an English target domain without paired recordings. The study uses 242 Asian-accented English recordings and 579 English recordings from the Speech Accent Archive and compares MFCC vectors, spectrogram images, and MFCC images. The original recordings were randomly partitioned into speaker-disjoint training, validation, and test sets before feature extraction and segmentation. CycleGAN training used the training partition, and auxiliary CNNs were used to quantify classifier-based target-domain assignment rather than direct accent-conversion accuracy. Supplementary CNN cross-validation used the combined training and validation representations, with the separate test partition excluded from fold construction. For Asian-to-English translation using MFCC images, 92% of the 100 evaluated generated representations were classified as English by the auxiliary CNN. This 92% value applies only to the Asian-to-English MFCC-image configuration and represents classifier-based target-domain reclassification. It does not directly measure perceptual accent reduction, intelligibility, waveform quality, linguistic-content preservation, or speaker-identity preservation. The MFCC-image configuration yielded the highest observed Asian-to-English target-domain reclassification rate under the evaluated settings; this does not establish intrinsic superiority of MFCC images. The results document configuration-specific target-domain assignments of CycleGAN-generated representations under the auxiliary classifier. Further work should include external evaluation, waveform reconstruction, ASR-based measures, listener studies, and balanced per-L1 analyses.

CycleGAN training used the training partition, and auxiliary CNNs were used to quantify classifier-based target-domain assignment rather than direct accent-conversion accuracy. Supplementary CNN cross-validation used the combined training and validation representations, with the separate test partition excluded from fold construction. For Asian-to-English translation using MFCC images, 92% of the 100 evaluated generated representations were classified as English by the auxiliary CNN. This 92% value applies only to the Asian-to-English MFCC-image configuration and represents classifier-based target-domain reclassification. It does not directly measure perceptual accent reduction, intelligibility, waveform quality, linguistic-content preservation, or speaker-identity preservation. The MFCC-image configuration yielded the highest observed Asian-to-English target-domain reclassification rate under the evaluated settings; this does not establish intrinsic superiority of MFCC images. The results document configuration-specific target-domain assignments of CycleGAN-generated representations under the auxiliary classifier. Further work should include external evaluation, waveform reconstruction, ASR-based measures, listener studies, and balanced per-L1 analyses.

title: SAS Multimetric Tribunal: What a Hallucination Benchmark Measures, and What It Does Not A Format-Controlled Audit of Structural Classification
abstract: Hallucination-detection systems are usually judged by a single headline metric, computed under a benchmark design that determines what that metric can show. This paper’s contribution is not a detection algorithm — structural coherence scoring is established — but a methodology for measuring exactly what a benchmark proves and what it does not, applied to the SAS Multimetric Tribunal: a seven-module, GPU-free structural classifier combining lexical, entity-mutation, curvature, and logical-inversion signals via a cascading multiplicative penalty (\(\kappa_{D} = 0.56\), \(\kappa_{R} = 0.15\)). On a stratified 1,800-pair benchmark (HaluEval-Dialogue, HaluEval-QA, TruthfulQA), the tribunal reaches F1 = 98.99% with zero false positives under an A\(\rightarrow\)A identical-text sanity check. We report this figure and then show, using a format-controlled negative (N1) on the same 1,800 IDs, that it measures format asymmetry between source and response rather than hallucination detection. The tribunal flags 1,569 of 1,800 verbatim correct answers presented alone (87.2%), and in HaluEval-QA scores the correct answer as _more_ anomalous than the hallucinated response. Three further findings follow from the same audit. (i) A per-module analysis shows the tribunal has no content-sensitive module in its current set: the one module designed to capture semantic divergence (cre_isi) gives the same per-ID score whether the response is byte-identical or completely different. (ii) The 87.97-point advantage of multiplicative combination over weighted averaging reported in v4 is an artifact of threshold calibration; under per-scheme thresholds on format-matched negatives, both schemes converge to F1 \(\approx 0.69\) and the multiplicative scheme is worse by AUROC. (iii) Adding a semantic-equivalence guard makes the tribunal and a Jaccard baseline statistically indistinguishable (F1 0.720 vs. 0.722; AUROC 0.881 vs. 0.881), because the guard’s apparent success depends on a constructional property of the control (the correct answer is a substring of the source by definition) rather than on content detection. The paper’s contribution is the audit procedure that produced these retirements. Four of v4’s quantitative claims do not survive it. What does survive — thresholds, the \(\kappa_{R}\) sweep, the forensic audit of v2 metrics, the per-module architecture itself as a diagnostic instrument — is reported with the same standard.

title: Can Artificial Intelligence Personalize Learning? An Analysis of AI-Based Adaptive Learning Systems for Senior School Students
abstract: Most classrooms still move at one speed. A teacher with thirty or forty students has to choose a pace that suits the middle of the class, which leaves weaker students behind and keeps stronger students waiting. AI-based adaptive learning systems promise to change this by watching how each student answers, estimating what that student already knows, and choosing the next task to match. This paper examines how far that promise holds for senior school students. It explains how adaptive systems work in simple terms, reviews findings from major meta-analyses and field experiments, including a randomised study of the Mindspark program in Delhi, and compares adaptive learning with the traditional one-size-fits-all approach. The evidence suggests that well-designed adaptive systems produce real and sometimes large learning gains, with reported effect sizes between about 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations, and that students who are furthest behind often gain the most. However, the gains depend heavily on how the system is designed and how it is used. Systems that simply give answers can weaken learning, and results shrink when teachers are not involved. The paper concludes that AI can personalise practice, feedback and pacing to a significant extent, but it cannot replace the motivational, social and judgement-based work of a teacher. A blended model, in which AI handles adaptive practice and teachers use the data to guide instruction, is proposed for Indian senior schools.

title: Star-ov: satellite-oriented trusted authorization and responsibility with stratified model encryption and ownership verifications
abstract: Abstract With the increasing adoption of deep neural networks (DNNs) in remote sensing interpretation and on-orbit intelligent processing, protecting the intellectual property of deployed models faces new challenges, including limited onboard computational resources, constrained satellite–ground communication bandwidth, differentiated multi-user services, and difficulty in ownership attribution after model leakage. Existing model protection approaches mainly rely on either active encryption or passive watermarking mechanisms, which are insufficient to simultaneously satisfy the requirements of access control, service continuity, and post-leakage accountability in satellite-based scenarios. In this paper, we propose STAR-OV, a stratified and controllable model protection framework tailored for satellite deployment. By introducing a two-stage reversible parameter perturbation mechanism, STAR-OV enables progressive degradation of model performance from the original high-accuracy state to an intermediate-accuracy state and finally to a fully unusable state. The perturbations introduced at different stages are organized into distributable hierarchical keys, thereby supporting differentiated service access for users with varying authorization levels. Furthermore, after the model is fully restored to its original accuracy, a latent watermark is embedded. The watermark remains inactive during normal inference without the activation key, while producing stable and verifiable responses on a trigger set once the corresponding key is applied, enabling reliable ownership verification in the event of model leakage. Experimental results on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces the usability of unauthorized models by modifying an extremely small fraction of parameters, while maintaining strong robustness against fine-tuning, pruning, and weight noise attacks. Owing to its low computational overhead and flexible deployment capability, STAR-OV provides a practical solution for resource-constrained satellite-based onboard intelligent inference scenarios.

title: UniLAP: A Unified Latent Action Policy for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.

title: Covering Radius and Deep Holes of Hyperderivative Reed-Solomon Codes under the NRT Metric
abstract: The deep hole problem is a fundamental problem in coding theory, and it has many important applications in code constructions and cryptography. The deep hole problem of Reed-Solomon codes has gained a lot of attention. As a generalization of Reed-Solomon codes under Hamming metric, we study the covering radius and deep holes of Hyperderivative Reed-Solomon (HRS) codes under the Niederreiter-Rosenbloom-Tsfasman (NRT) metric. We determine the NRT covering radius of HRS code and characterize its NRT deep holes via Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) extensions and polynomial remainder conditions. We further relate the enumeration of NRT deep holes to the characteristic polynomial of an associated hyperplane arrangement. We also provide three classes of explicit NRT deep-hole constructions, propose a Cheng-Murray type conjecture for HRS codes under the NRT metric and obtain a conditional low-layer description. Using these characterizations, we derive exact enumeration formulas in several special cases.

title: Not Every Cue Is Evidence: Cue Supportability for Forensic Distillation in Face Forgery Detection
abstract: Explainable face forgery detection requires not only correct judgments but also forensic evidence supported by the input image. However, training cues are typically derived from the forgery generation pipeline. Since images available to the model are of limited quality and resolution, it is difficult to observe the fine-grained traces these cues refer to. Training methods that further supply such cues as privileged supervision exacerbate the problem, as the student is taught to articulate evidence it cannot perceive. The student consequently resorts to templated or over-generalized expressions, giving rise to the correct-answer, wrong-evidence (CAWE) failure. We propose a dual supportability audit that filters privileged cues before distillation. Each candidate cue must be predictable from the remaining privileged context and causally tied to high-attribution visual regions in the current image. Only cues satisfying both conditions receive substantial distillation weight, preventing unsupported details from leaking into the student. Experiments across eight benchmarks show that our method maintains or improves detection accuracy while significantly raising explanation faithfulness compared to existing paradigms.

title: Exploration strategies for Gaussian process bandit optimization with inference regret guarantees
abstract: Existing cumulative regret guarantees for Bayesian optimization (BO) do not necessarily characterize the quality of the algorithm's final output. This gap is critical under noisy evaluations, where the goal is to return a single high-quality recommendation. To address it, we introduce efficient exploration strategies that can be incorporated into any BO procedure by occasionally replacing the acquisition query with an exploration query. To validate this approach, we bound the Gaussian process posterior standard deviation over the search space via the fill distance of the queries, which measures the largest region left unexplored. We then use this result to derive upper bounds on the inference regret, i.e., the gap between the global optimum and the function value at the algorithm's returned point. Empirically, these exploration strategies improve the final recommendations of existing BO algorithms on synthetic benchmarks, hyperparameter optimization, and a control task.

title: Designing A Human-Governed Agentic Project Management Model: A Closed-Loop Architecture for Autonomous Project Intelligence, Decision Control and Human–AI Teaming
abstract: Purpose: This article develops a Human Governed Agentic Project Management (HG-APM) model for integrating autonomous AI capabilities with human project management authority. Design/methodology/approach: An integrative conceptual synthesis combines four literature streams: AI-enabled project management, autonomous Manager Agents, human oversight governance, and human–AI teaming. Source supported findings are separated from conceptual inferences, and the resulting architecture is expressed as a closed-loop model. Findings: The model comprises Sense, Understand, Diagnose, Predict, Plan, Evaluate, Authorize, Act, Monitor, Learn and Replan. It proposes a consequence sensitive, graduated autonomy rather than a single autonomy level. Routine and reversible actions may be automated within predefined boundaries, whereas consequential financial, contractual, scope, safety, stakeholder, reputational and strategic decisions require stronger authority from the designated human or organizational decisionmaker. Originality: The model integrates project-management intelligence, human–AI teaming and governance into one operational architecture. It contributes to a project specific decision boundary and testable propositions for evaluating whether governed agentic AI improves project outcomes without weakening human control.

title: An Ontology Construction Framework for Asset Lifecycle Management: Agentic Travelling Approach with Field Application in Shale Oil Wellbore Maintenance
abstract: Abstract The rapid deployment of AI-native applications in complex wellbore operations requires unified, high-quality data integration to sustain continuous model evolution and reliable asset lifecycle management. However, heterogeneity in standards, semantics, and system architectures across legacy operational datasets limits their immediate applicability for dynamic and agile AI workflows. In alignment with the digital transformation priorities on information management, knowledge integration, and emerging technology implementations, this study develops a Human- and Entity-Centric Agentic Travelling Approach (HATA) for constructing dynamic-static ontology that support adaptive, cross-scenario data integration. This supports the energy transformation by enabling adaptive data integration for complex decision scenarios, validated through 3 typical types of downhole failure cases. HATA introduces a self-organising ontology construction framework composed of three specialised AI agents configured to address data quality challenges in knowledge modelling, and semantic enabled data integration. The planner interprets engineer-determined themes and decomposes them into ontology construction tasks; the traveller explores latent representational spaces to generate ontology candidates optimised for scenario relevance; and the supervisor assesses structural and semantic consistency, providing iterative feedback to guide refinement. The approach was evaluated using operational datasets (2021-2024) from 45 shale-oil wellbores in western China, focusing on wax deposition, scaling, and pump leakage, with corresponding financial management. More than 40 multi-modal parameters including deviation surveys, dynamometer cards, electrical parameters, inspection logs, operational and maintenance (O&M) alarms, and workover records were mapped through the HATA semantic and compared with expert curated benchmarks using a similarity threshold of 0.8 to quantify semantic alignment and structural completeness. Across all evaluated scenarios, the agentic ontology builder demonstrated substantial improvements in interpretability, operational efficiency, and data assembly performance. User intent comprehension achieved expect accuracy, with a single misinterpretation observed. Task planning precision approached optimal levels, while ontology construction cycles were completed within 40 seconds to 2 minutes, requiring minimal supervisory adjustments. Generated datasets reached an average semantic similarity exceeding 0.82 compared with field engineer benchmarks. Importantly, the resulting dynamic ontologies reduced decision-making time for failure diagnosis from approximately 1.5 hours to ≤10 minutes per case. These outcomes demonstrate the potential of HATA to benefit asset lifecycle management and strengthen AI-enabled operational workflows envisioned for wellbore intelligent transformation. This work introduces an innovative agentic travelling methodology for ontology construction, representing a novel innovation of genAI agentic system for ontology and knowledge modelling within shale oil wellbore downhole operations. Unlike static ontology, HATA also supports continuous evolution through digital-twin-driven updates, enabling the generation of adaptive "data blueprints" for predictive analytics. By bridging fragmented legacy datasets with emergent AI workflows, the methodology advances data science priorities in new technology deployment, valuation, and knowledge management, offering a scalable pathway for future energy transformation capabilities.

title: Does Retrieval Relevance Matter for AI-Generated Book Introductions? A Matched-Random Memory Evaluation
abstract: Digital libraries are exploring LLMs for reading-promotion services such as automatically generated book introductions. A tempting design is to retrieve relevant accumulated reader feedback at generation time. We test this in a zero-human-subject controlled experiment: a librarian agent generates introductions for 32 held-out test books under three conditions (No Memory, a composition-matched random-memory control, and Relevant Memory, operationalized through embedding similarity and genre matching), judged on four criteria by a separate-model LLM (GPT-4o). The key methodological device is the composition-matched random-memory control, which isolates retrieval relevance from mere context presence. Lexical uptake checks confirm that retrieved memory is incorporated into generated introductions. Relevant Memory shows no LLM-judged advantage over No Memory on the composite outcome, but outperforms Matched-Random Memory on hook quality (Δ = 0.125, 95% CI [0.023, 0.250]). This pattern suggests that retrieval selection may matter when additional memory is introduced, rather than providing a general improvement over a strong no-memory baseline. We frame the study as pipeline validity evidence rather than evidence of improved human-perceived quality.

title: A Time-Synchronous Prequential Evaluation Framework for Next-Week Student Disengagement Prediction from Moodle LMS Logs
abstract: Retrospective evaluation of early-warning models may not reflect information available when predictions are issued and outcomes become observable. We developed a time-synchronous prequential framework for online prediction of next-week student disengagement, operationalised as inactivity onset, from Moodle logs. Ordered by calendar time, models were updated only with available outcomes and remained unchanged for all predictions at each prediction cutoff; development, calibration and evaluation were chronologically separate. We compared stochastic gradient descent logistic regression (SGD-LR), online sequential extreme learning machine (OSELM) and echo state network (ESN) across predictive performance, fixed, frozen and rolling threshold policies, calendar-time variation and four behavioural feature sets. Held-out evaluation comprised 49,329 predictions with 37.68% inactivity-onset prevalence. Discrimination was similar (average precision 0.665-0.679; ROC-AUC 0.755-0.774). OSELM had the highest recall, SGD-LR the highest precision and specificity, and ESN the highest Matthews correlation coefficient and balanced accuracy. Lower thresholds increased recall and alert volume, whereas rolling adaptation did not improve MCC over frozen thresholds. Weekly performance and calibrated-probability distributions varied without sustained deterioration. During model selection, cumulative-and-temporal features achieved the highest individual-set AP, with modest gains from combining all feature groups. These findings indicate that streaming early-warning evaluation should consider calibration, threshold-dependent performance, alert burden and calendar-time variation alongside aggregate discrimination.

title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.

title: Universal Distributed Feature Extraction Complementary to Side Information via H-Score
abstract: This paper considers a distributed estimation system where edge nodes transmit averaged features to a center node for parameter estimation. A key challenge arises when the center node possesses auxiliary side information: how to design local extractors that are universally optimal for any downstream task, while avoiding redundancy with the side information. To tackle this problem, we orthogonally decompose the joint function space and demonstrate in the weak-dependence regime that the modal decomposition of the canonical dependence kernel's conditional-additive component yields optimal, task-independent features. We construct a distributed nested H-score to learn this decomposition and show that, under a limited feature budget, the mean-squared error (MSE) gap to the best task-specific features is determined solely by the task's alignment with the discarded, least informative modes, and vanishes to leading order for every square-integrable task once the budget is sufficient.

title: AI-Powered Adaptive Learning and Smart Education Platform
abstract: Education is becoming increasingly digital, yet many students still face difficulties in understanding complex concepts, remembering long answers, identifying their learning gaps, and preparing effectively for examinations. This paper presents an AI-powered adaptive learning platform designed to provide personalized and interactive learning support. The system uses Artificial Intelligence to explain questions in detail, generate short exam-oriented answers and recall keywords, analyze students' performance, identify knowledge gaps, and recommend suitable learning tasks. The platform also provides 3D visualization for mathematical and geometric concepts, AI-assisted learning for languages such as Marathi and Sanskrit with Hindi and English explanations, AI-based viva examination, instant tests, PDF/notes-based learning, progress tracking, and gamification. The main aim is to make learning personalized, understandable, interactive, and focused on actual student improvement rather than simply providing answers

title: Outlier Detection for Shale Gas Production Data: An Integrated Approach of Enhanced Clustering and Domain Knowledge
abstract: Abstract Shale gas production data are inherently non-stationary, characterized by distinct decline trends across various production stages. These datasets are frequently contaminated with outliers stemming from operational interventions, such as well shut-ins and choke adjustments, as well as sensor malfunctions and human-induced collection errors. Consequently, robust outlier detection is a prerequisite for reliable production data analysis. While unsupervised learning algorithms, such as Local Outlier Factor (LOF), Angle-Based Outlier Detection (ABOD), and Isolation Forest (IF), are currently employed, their efficacy is often hindered by the subjectivity involved in defining manual thresholds for anomaly partitioning. This study develops an enhanced unsupervised classification algorithm, termed IF-K-Medoids, by integrating the IF algorithm with K-Medoids clustering. This hybrid algorithm addresses the initialization sensitivity of K-Medoids by leveraging IF to optimally select initial cluster centers, thereby eliminating the need for random or manual selection. Furthermore, the K-Medoids enables automated differentiation between anomalous and normal samples, overcoming the subjectivity of manual thresholding. This algorithm is then incorporated into a two-stage outlier detection approach that fuses machine learning with domain knowledge. IF-K-Medoids performs an initial screening of outliers, which are then further reviewed using domain knowledge. This two-stage outlier detection approach enhances both the accuracy and reliability of identifying outliers in production data. The IF-K-Medoids algorithm was first validated using datasets from the University of California-Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning Repository, achieving an Area Under the Curve (AUC) exceeding 0.88, which outperforms standalone IF and Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) algorithms. The proposed two-stage outlier detection approach was subsequently validated using field data from two shale gas wells. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach produced physically interpretable detection results, thereby facilitating improvements in the accuracy and precision of production forecasting, reserves estimation, and rate transient analysis for shale gas wells.

title: LimAgents: Multi-Agent LLMs for Generating Research Limitations
abstract: Identifying scientific limitations is essential for transparent reporting and rigorous critical appraisal. However, zero-shot large language models (LLMs) often produce generic critiques, repeat author-stated limitations, and overlook paper-specific methodological and contextual weaknesses. We propose LimAgents, a training-free multi-agent framework in which role-specialized workers extract explicit limitations, analyze methodological weaknesses, adopt a peer-review perspective, and examine cited literature. Workers can refine their outputs through feedback from a Leader Agent, after which a Master Agent consolidates and de-duplicates the resulting limitations; ablations show that refinement benefits GPT-4o mini but not Llama 3 8B. For evaluation, we construct a validated, non-exhaustive reference set by combining author-stated limitations with OpenReview critiques and decomposing them into atomic Limitation Units through multi-model consensus. We evaluate generated limitations using human-calibrated, LU-level semantic matching with two independent LLM judges. Across multiple backbones, LimAgents achieves the highest F1 across both baseline-comparison backbones. In terms of reference-aligned coverage, it achieves improvements of 4.41 and 15.51 points over the Llama 3 8B and GPT-4o mini zero-shot configurations, respectively. Furthermore, LimAgents yields substantial gains in overall F1 scores, exceeding competing baselines by 12.30–20.91 points when utilizing Mistral 7B, and 5.31–34.18 points with Qwen 2.5 3B. title: Multimodal spatiotemporal knowledge graph construction for conflict-event analysis: an integrated framework with geographic entity-map association
abstract: Heterogeneous conflict-event information is distributed across textual reports, web images, and scanned maps, making it difficult to represent entities, events, geographic locations, temporal attributes, and multimedia evidence within a unified knowledge graph. This study proposes an integrated framework for constructing multimodal spatiotemporal knowledge graphs from event-oriented heterogeneous data. The framework combines textual entity, relation, and event extraction; visual object detection; scanned-map coordinate recognition; geographic entity grounding; cross-modal entity fusion; provenance-aware storage; and graph visualization. A cascaded YOLOv5-PaddleOCR procedure first detects and crops coordinate annotation regions from scanned maps and then reconstructs the map extent from the recognized coordinates. Textual place entities are geocoded using GeoNames and linked to relevant maps through point-polygon spatial intersection. Quantitative experiments showed F1-scores of 0.76-0.84 for the evaluated text extraction tasks. For aircraft, ship, and general web-image detection, YOLOv8 obtained mAP@0.5 values of 0.935, 0.890, and 0.922, respectively. On the 287-map scanned-map dataset, YOLOv5 achieved a region-detection F1-score of 0.977. In the 278-map paired out-of-fold OCR evaluation, complete map-coordinate recognition increased from 64.03% with direct PaddleOCR to 87.05% with the cascaded procedure, and the paired difference was statistically significant (exact McNemar test, p < 0.001). Under an event- and source-document-grouped evaluation protocol, the complete constrained cross-modal entity-fusion method achieved an F1-score of 0.884. A conflict-event case study further demonstrates the practical applicability of the framework.

title: TorchSpin: Differentiable Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Simulation in PyTorch
abstract: Interpreting electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra commonly requires repeated forward simulation and optimization of spin Hamiltonian parameters. Established software provides mature simulation and fitting methods, but these calculations are not generally available as differentiable components within machine-learning workflows. We present TorchSpin, an open-source PyTorch framework that ports the organization and numerical conventions of EasySpin into a tensor-based computational environment. Representative calculations spanning continuous-wave EPR, ENDOR, pulse EPR, spin dynamics, trajectory simulation, and magnetometry closely reproduced corresponding EasySpin results. In matched benchmarks, TorchSpin CPU execution was faster than EasySpin for six of nine workloads although performance depended strongly on the calculation. We therefore focused on the capabilities enabled by automatic differentiation in PyTorch. In a Cu(II) powder-spectrum demonstration, feedback propagated through TorchSpin improved the quality of a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) without using parameter labels during refinement. Models trained from randomly initialized CNNs using only noisy spectra and TorchSpin reconstruction loss achieved median similarities of $\geq$ 0.99. CNNs trained on TorchSpin-generated libraries also transferred without adaptation to independently generated EasySpin spectra with performance comparable to EasySpin-trained controls. Once trained, the CNN produced initial parameter estimates in approximately 1 ms per spectrum while a batch of 512 was processed in approximately 1.3 ms with GPU acceleration. TorchSpin therefore provides both a tested Python implementation of established EPR calculations and a differentiable physical layer for rapid learned inference, spectral refinement, and parameter-label-free training.

title: CodeLift: Your Test Suite Is Secretly a Dense SWE Curriculum
abstract: The pass-all-test binary reward has become a standard recipe for training software engineering agents, but its sparsity eliminates difference of partially correct patches. The test pass-rate is a natural alternative. However, we find that it is not a reliable indicator of patch quality. A functionality being tested can be covered by either one challenging test or one hundred trivial tests, where the majority might be already satisfied pass-to-pass tests. We introduce CodeLift, a reinforcement learning method that dynamically calibrates pass-rate rewards, turning the test suite into an adaptive curriculum. At each iteration, CodeLift groups tests that kill the same patches and patches that pass the same tests, then gives more weight to test groups that fewer patch groups pass. This reduces the impact of majority simple tests and focuses more on what is still challenging. Within each rollout, CodeLift applies the same scoring rule to repository snapshots, assigning credit to useful actions even when later ones introduce regressions. Experiments on SWE benchmarks show that CodeLift consistently improves pass@1/2/4/8 over binary and pass-rate baselines. Analyses show that CodeLift provides dense, stable learning signals and unlocks the inherent curriculum in the test suite.

title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part I: Glauber Dynamics
abstract: In the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem, we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\{\pm1\}^N$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. We show that Glauber dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization, demonstrating that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

evidence.title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part I: Glauber Dynamics
evidence.abstract: In the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem, we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\{\pm1\}^N$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. We show that Glauber dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization, demonstrating that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

title: DIGS: Distribution-Informed Gaussian Splatting for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation
abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian segmentation typically binds semantic features to the per-Gaussian state via per-scene gradient training (1-4 h) or the more recent closed-form distillation. Both commit each primitive to a single feature; therefore, boundary Gaussians spanning multiple 2D instances are forced into a hard decision that degrades retrieval accuracy and yields unstable mask boundaries at render time. We present DIGS, a training-free framework with two stages, class-agnostic mapping and multi-modal encoding, that decouples instance discovery from linguistic naming. At the Gaussian level, our distribution-informed representation maintains an explicit top-$M$ label distribution per primitive, updated by a tempered Dirichlet rule; preservation of multi-peaked label distributions at boundary primitives allows a late-argmax renderer to recover clean instance boundaries. A bidirectional state machine aggregates these distributions into a persistent class-agnostic instance ontology. The instance-level encoding stage then fuses the CLIP visual embedding of each instance's isolated 3D footprint with the CLIP-text embedding of an LLM-generated attribute description, disambiguating visually similar instances. On a single A100, DIGS completes mapping and instance encoding on LERF-OVS in 1.0-3.2 min per scene, depending on whether LLM fusion is enabled, and serves native 3D queries in 5.4 ms. It reaches 71.95% mean mIoU on LERF-OVS, outperforming both the training-free SFS and training-based LaGa baselines. DIGS also achieves the highest mean mIoU on LERF-Mask and 3D-OVS and surpasses Gaga and ObjectGS on Replica under their respective evaluation protocols. Code is available at https://github.com/ZephyrZos/DIGS.

title: Confidential Error-Correcting Codes
abstract: We introduce Confidential Error-correcting Codes (CECs), a new cryptographic primitive that enables reliable decoding from perturbed codewords while preserving message confidentiality. We formalize this primitive through three security properties: confidentiality, robustness, and soundness. To realize this goal, we develop a general framework for constructing CECs based on a Randomness-Security Separation (RSS) structure, which first encodes a nonce to introduce randomness and then masks the encoded payload with a pseudorandom function. Based on our RSS framework, we instantiate CECs, called Conc-CEC, using concatenated Reed-Muller and Reed-Solomon codes. The resulting Conc-CEC admits provable guarantees for all three properties. Notably, compared to PRCs (CRYPTO'24), another recent cryptographic primitive with error-correcting capability, CECs achieve significantly stronger concrete security guarantees under practical parameter settings. As a primary application of CECs, we further present CECMark, a watermarking scheme for AI-generated images. Our experiments on real-world generative image models show that CECMark consistently outperforms state-of-the-art watermarking methods, including Gaussian Shading (CVPR'24), PRCMark (ICLR'25), and T2SMark (NeurIPS'25). In particular, CECMark achieves higher robustness across all 56 evaluated perturbations and ensures a false positive rate below $10^{-5}$ without introducing side effects. Taken together, our work lays a novel cryptographic foundation for trustworthy watermarking schemes that, for the first time, unify provable security guarantees with strong practical reliability.

title: CLEAR-FORCE: A reservoir computing framework for closed-loop brain stimulation
abstract: Abstract Electrical stimulation of brain activity has emerged as a key therapeutic intervention for neurological diseases. The success of these approaches relies on precisely tuned stimulation parameters. A major challenge is that these parameters should ideally be adjusted in real-time based on changes in brain activity. Closed-loop controllers address this challenge by monitoring brain activity and adapting stimulation according to ongoing changes in neural dynamics. While machine learning has been helpful in this context, closed-loop controllers typically do not adapt in real-time to fluctuations in brain activity. Here, we propose a novel framework based on reservoir computing to train a closed-loop, real-time neural controller. This approach, termed CLEAR-FORCE, trains the output weights of a recurrent network based on a combination of target signals and feedback from brain activity. Two series of simulations were performed, where the controller was successful at (1) inducing neural oscillations in a population of spiking neurons and (2) suppressing pathological oscillations. This framework provides a promising avenue for the implementation of neural controllers in low-powered, real-time, and adaptive hardware that harnesses machine learning for the personalized treatment of brain disorders.

title: NLP-Based Student Readability Assessment and Personalized Feedback System
abstract: Student writing assessment is important in academic learning, but manual evaluation of written responses can require considerable time and may provide limited information about specific writing difficulties. This paper presents an NLP-Based Student Readability Assessment and Personalized Feedback System for automated analysis of student English writing. The system allows users to enter text directly or upload PDF, DOCX, and TXT documents. Submitted content is analyzed for readability, grammar, spelling, vocabulary, sentence structure, and text statistics. Seven readability measures are used to estimate reading difficulty, while vocabulary richness, repeated words, difficult words, sentence length, and sentence type provide additional writing characteristics. The system combines these results to generate an overall writing-quality score and a feature-weighted proficiency estimate. Personalized suggestions explain detected weaknesses and recommend areas for improvement. Teacher-managed assignments with reference answers and student submissions are also supported. Analysis records are stored per user in a lightweight database.

title: TSI-CORE-1.0-RC2: supporting repository and verification files
abstract: TSI-CORE 1.0-RC2 — Public Research Release Candidate Author: Igor Chechelnitsky ORCID: 0009-0007-4607-1946 Project: Theory of Structural Invariants (TSI-CORE) Original specification date: 30 July 2026 Release status: Public preprint candidate for independent scientific review. Overview TSI-CORE introduces a minimal formal kernel for representations and partial transformations, formulated in classical many-sorted first-order logic with equality. The specification addresses structural equivalence, partial action, declared composition, and a distinguished unit transformation through six mandatory axiom groups. The mathematical kernel deliberately does not assume physical reality, consciousness, time, dynamics, probability, memory, or any particular computational implementation. Included editions Four complementary reading editions are provided: Scientific specification — English (normative mathematical source) Scientific exposition — Russian Accessible explanation — English Accessible explanation — Russian The repository additionally includes the canonical RC2 specification, historical audit materials, finite-model verification scripts, reference outputs, and checksums. Verification and limitations Eight explicitly constructed finite examples have passed the included automated checker, covering the minimal model, axiom-independence witnesses, and an optional structural-preservation counterexample. These checks do not constitute complete machine-verified proofs, experimental validation, or independent peer review. Independent UTS audit The release also invites independent assessment of potential relationships between TSI and the UTS architecture. The audit investigates whether specific UTS mechanisms can be faithfully interpreted as extensions of TSI-CORE. Security properties involving consensus, concurrency, nullifiers, DAG ancestry, privacy, and bridge atomicity require independent assumptions and verification. No claim of UTS correctness is implied by the existence of TSI-CORE. Research integrity This release is a frozen public research candidate. Mathematical corrections must be documented and versioned rather than silently modifying the normative specification. Independent counterexamples, formalization attempts, references to prior work, and reproducible critical evaluations are welcome. Repository: https://github.com/Muhomor2/TSI-CORE Zenodo DOI: Pending archival registration. License: To be explicitly selected by the author before final publication.

title: A Speech-to-Knowledge Framework for Archaic Thai Language Understanding and Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: Digitizing oral cultural heritage necessitates computational methods capable of bridging the acoustic, orthographic, and semantic gaps between historical and contemporary language forms. This study proposes a cascaded Automatic Speech Recognition–Neural Machine Translation–Knowledge Graph (ASR–NMT–KG) framework designed to transcribe archaic Thai recitations, translate them into modern Thai, and subsequently convert their semantic content into structured knowledge. The framework was evaluated utilizing the Thai Ancient Medical Speech Corpus (TAMSC), which comprises 14000 original and augmented utterances from ten certified Thai Traditional Medicine practitioners. The domain-adapted ASR model achieved a word error rate (WER) of 8.3%, a character error rate (CER) of 4.8%, and an Archaic Orthography Error Rate (AOER) of 6.2%. The mT5-Large translation model obtained a BLEU score of 51.7, while the Knowledge Graph construction module achieved an F1-score of 0.89. Furthermore, the WER exhibited a strong negative association with translation quality (Pearson’s r = −0.87, p < 0.001), providing empirical evidence of cross-stage performance dependency within the cascaded pipeline. These results indicate that the cascaded architecture offers an accurate, modular, and interpretable approach for preserving and semantically exploring low-resource historical language materials.

title: HATA: Multi-Agent Ontology Framework for High-Quality Log Interpretation Data Reconstruct in Existed Wells Re-Assessment
abstract: Abstract This study addresses the challenge of re-evaluating existed CNPC wells, where considerable potentials remain underestimated due to historical technological limitations and inconsistent interpretation workflows. In resources-scarce regions, existed well reassessment is essential for resource optimisation and supports the digital transformation of wells lifecycle management. This process relies on multi-modal data integration, including logs, interpretation charts, expert knowledge, and historical data, however, data inconsistencies, incompleteness, and semantic heterogeneity reduce analytical accuracy and impede value creation from data. To overcome these barriers, we propose an ontology-driven, multi-agent allied framework that autonomously re-constructs unified, high-quality datasets. The framework enables standardised data acquisition, intelligent quality control, missing-data and knowledge interpolation, and automated log processing, ensuring reliable and interpretable data supply throughout the re-assessment workflow among existed wells re-evaluation. We introduce the Human and Entity-centric Agent Travelling based Ontology Constructing (HATA) approach, an ontology based methodology aligned with knowledge management and intelligent system development. HATA employs a multi-agent architecture with 3 roles: the planner for task planning and orchestration, the traveller for ontology network construction through latent space "travelling," and the supervisor for validation and refinement. Agents first generate 3 most-possbile candidate ontology networks through digital-twin-based hypothesis testing, supported by data mining and data semantic management techniques. After agentic travelling to select optimal ontology, the system extracts log data, performs structural and semantic quality checks, interpolates missing values and link expert knowledge gaps, and executes log evaluation tasks. The outcomes guide iterative ontology refinement. Human-in-loop (HIL) interactions are supported through natural language and multi modal interfaces, enabling controllability and transparent reasoning consistent with engineering intent. Validation on 10 CNPC existed wells evaluated semantic understanding, task planning, ontology accuracy, data consistency, missing data interpolation, and reasoning completeness. Engineers assessed outputs using α ≥0.80 semantic similarity threshold across 3 interaction levels: Low (1–15 rounds), Mild (15–30), and High (30+). Intent comprehension and planning precision improved with interaction depth, demonstrating adaptive learning. More accurate ontology modelling strengthened fault tolerance for data compensation and hypothetical reasoning, though expert oversight remained essential for edge cases. Overall reasoning completeness, defined as ≥75% content judged reasonable, increased from 6 wells (Low) to 9 wells (High), confirming HATA's effectiveness as a controllable, interpretable assistant and its potential for deployment as an emerging technology in field operations. The results conclude that the manuscript presents a novel multi-agent framework for dynamic ontology modelling and automated dataset reconstructing tailored to existed well reassessment. By integrating role-specific agents, genAI, and ontology, the approach offers scalable, fault tolerant, and interpretable knowledge management. Its capabilities in task planning, iterative refinement, and "reasonable imagination" support reliable decision making and contribute directly to upstream digitalisation and emerging technology valuation. The methodology is believed extensible to other complex oilfield operations, providing a practical pathway for digital asset lifecycle enhancement.

title: Structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics for partial differential equations
abstract: Machine learning surrogates of partial differential equations (PDEs) are commonly trained on data generated by numerical solvers. Therefore, the training data obey not the PDE but the modified equation of the numerical scheme, and the test loss, computed on data from the same solver, cannot distinguish a model that learned the physics from one that learned the discretization error. Here, we show that the difference is nevertheless visible in the trained model. We propose a suite of structure-preserving fidelity diagnostics, simple scores that measure whether a learned model respects one known property of the physics, such as a conserved quantity, a symmetry or a Hamiltonian structure, without access to the training data or the governing equation. Over five systems, the diagnostics track the error with respect to the true dynamics with a rank correlation of up to $0.94$, while the test loss is uncorrelated or anti-correlated with it. For the Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries and Navier-Stokes equations, the diagnostics separate numerical schemes that the test loss ranks as equivalent, including schemes of the same order. order.

title: Compute-optimal data scaling for neural surrogates via multi-fidelity training
abstract: Neural surrogates for Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) are usually trained on synthetic data from numerical simulators. As models grow and scaling laws demand larger datasets, the cost of data generation often outweighs the training cost and becomes the bottleneck in the scaling quest. Unlike data in other domains, however, each PDE sample has a tunable cost that depends on its numerical fidelity, with the resulting cost-accuracy trade-off governed by known convergence rates. We exploit this property by formalizing neural surrogate training as a function of both data quantity and fidelity under a fixed data generation compute budget, treating fidelity as a fine-grained discrete spectrum rather than a binary distinction. Building on this, we show that multi-fidelity training enables Pareto-optimal error scaling against data generation compute. By using simulations at lower fidelities as an additional training signal, training on the optimal fidelity mixture matches the accuracy of high-fidelity-only training, with up to $6.3\times$ less data generation compute across our settings. We validate these findings across six PDE problems spanning structured grids and unstructured meshes, two distinct error sources (discretization and iterative-solver error), and four surrogate architectures, totaling over 7,000 training runs.

title: DiTSG: Context-Aware Air Traffic Scene Generation with Multi-Agent Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Understanding how many aircraft, and which traffic configurations, can be safely and efficiently managed by air traffic controllers within a given airspace is fundamental to air traffic management. Air traffic controllers continuously modify aircraft trajectories through interventions such as speed advisories and radar vectoring, and the patterns of these interventions are difficult to capture effectively using existing air traffic simulators. To address this limitation, we propose Diffusion Transformers for Traffic Scene Generation (DiTSG), which learns to generate air traffic scenes from recorded multi-aircraft trajectories. DiTSG employs stacked multi-agent inverted Transformer layers as the denoising backbone of a diffusion transformer, jointly generates the trajectories of multiple aircraft within a traffic scene, and conditions the generation on agent-specific required times of arrival. The resulting trajectories generated by DiTSG preserve realistic inter-aircraft interactions observed in actual air traffic operations. Experiments show that the DiTSG generates diverse traffic scenes that reproduce the statistical properties of recorded traffic while preserving realistic inter-aircraft interactions.

title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
abstract: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.

evidence.title: CryptoFlowBench: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning on Blockchains for Cryptocurrency Fund Tracing
evidence.abstract: Pseudonymous accounts and complex smart-contract ecosystems substantially hinder the tracing of illicit cryptocurrency fund flows. Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved promising performance in blockchain fraud detection, yet their static node- or edge-level predictions do not naturally generalize to multi-hop fund tracing. Meanwhile, existing tracing methods mainly rely on predefined heuristics to capture multi-hop relationships, limiting their adaptive reasoning capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce CryptoFlowBench, a benchmark constructed from authoritative reports on cryptocurrency-related illicit incidents, with four tasks spanning local to multi-hop fund tracing. These tasks pose substantial challenges to existing learning- and heuristic-based methods, particularly in complex multi-hop scenarios. We therefore propose ChainSleuth, a graph-tool-augmented agent that iteratively reasons, invokes graph tools, and updates its tracing trajectory, enabling adaptive information acquisition and recovery from erroneous paths. Experiments show that no baseline consistently dominates all four tasks, revealing substantial gaps between local fraud detection and multi-hop fund tracing. ChainSleuth achieves notable improvements on multi-hop tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic graph reasoning for cryptocurrency fund investigation.

title: EgoAlign: Situated 3D Understanding without Situation Descriptions
abstract: Situated 3D Question Answering requires models to interpret a 3D scene relative to an agent's pose. Existing methods commonly convey that pose through a natural-language situation description, which may be unavailable or costly to obtain in real-world deployments. While some methods additionally incorporate numerical pose, we find that randomly shuffling the agent pose causes little performance degradation, indicating limited functional dependence on the numerical pose. To address this gap, we introduce EgoAlign, a simple 3D language model that represents a scene in an agent-centric coordinate frame, together with a dedicated egocentric alignment stage comprising four complementary tasks: object category recognition, egocentric direction prediction, metric distance estimation, and spatial relation prediction. This stage teaches the model to consistently interpret scene geometry relative to the agent's pose before task-specific fine-tuning. EgoAlign achieves the strongest performance on SQA3D, Real-3DQA, and MSQA among compared methods while remaining highly efficient. More importantly, removing textual situation descriptions yields comparable or better downstream performance, whereas shuffling EgoAlign's numerical pose causes substantial degradation. These results show that EgoAlign establishes agent-centric spatial context directly from numerical pose without requiring textual situation descriptions.

title: An Analytical Study of ML Models for Behavioral Analytics in Catching Suspicious Payroll Activity
abstract: Machine learning methods are essential for enhancing behavioural analytics, enabling automatic pattern discovery and adaptive learning.Supervised learning models benefit from detecting known instances of fraud when labeled data are available.In contrast, unsupervised and semi-supervised methods can detect previously unknown anomalies without clearly defined labels indicating whether the data are fraudulent.Furthermore, deep learning models, including autoencoders and recurrent neural networks, can learn complex, nonlinear, and temporal dependencies in payroll data.All these features enable machine learning-based systems to keep up with changes in payroll practices, the workforce, and fraud strategies, thereby enhancing detection accuracy and resilience.In practice, data imbalance, feature selection, model interpretability, scalability, and concept drift have a significant impact [7].Various machine learning models have different strengths and weaknesses based on the features of payroll data and operational limitations [8] [9].Consequently, an analytical study should be conducted systematically to determine the effectiveness of ML models in behavioural analytics for detecting suspicious payroll activity. A. Structure of the PaperThis paper is organized as follows: Section II payroll activity and suspicious activity analysis.Section III Behavioral analytic framework for payroll monitoring Section IV.Machine learning model for behavioral analysis.The literature review is presented in Section V, and the conclusions and prospective research are discussed in Section VI.

title: A Hybrid Agentic RAG Architecture with Knowledge Graphs and Text-to-SQL for Automating Citizen Services in a Public Scientific Institution
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible but incorrect content, a risk that is unacceptable when public institutions disclose scientific and legal information. This study presents and evaluates a hybrid agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system that automates first-level responses to citizen information requests at the Marine Institute of Peru (IMARPE). A baseline analysis of 196 requests showed a mean response time of 12 business days, above the 10-day legal limit, and identified 26.9% of them as routine, data-extractable queries. The system, developed under CRISP-DM, uses LangGraph to route each query to a LightRAG knowledge graph (Neo4j) built from institutional yearbooks, to a Text-to-SQL agent that queries the IMARSIS relational database through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), or to both, with Gemini 2.5 Flash as the foundation model and a referral protocol for out-of-scope requests. Five institutional domain experts rated 30 test cases, with mean scores of 4.45/5 for factual accuracy, 4.10/5 for completeness, and 4.57/5 for clarity. Mean end-to-end software latency was 20.43 s (maximum 49.20 s), and 30 pilot users rated usability at 80.42 on the System Usability Scale (Cronbach’s α = 0.96). These preliminary, single-site results indicate that combining graph-based and SQL-based grounding is feasible for routine citizen-information services; comparison with simpler baselines remains pending.

title: Can Large Language Models Identify Technical Terms in Documents Like Human Annotators?
abstract: Processing technical terms in documents is essential for digital libraries and knowledge organisation, supporting applications such as scholarly search, information retrieval, and domain terminology construction. While document-level term identification, a sub-task of automatic term extraction (ATE), has been tackled as a sequence labelling task, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) opens new avenues for prompt-based extraction. However, evaluation practices have persistently relied on simple success or failure against a single gold standard, without analysing how model behaviours align with human annotations, especially on borderline cases where annotators disagree. To address this issue, this study investigates to what extent LLMs can perform term identification using prompt instructions mirroring human annotator conditions. By evaluating multiple commercial and open-weight LLMs against double human annotations in ACL RD-TEC 2.0, an ATE benchmark, we show that LLMs achieve performance close to human annotators (up to 76.6% F1, within 5 percentage points of the inter-human agreement of 81.6%), with open-weight 30B-scale models outperforming larger commercial counterparts. Crucially, our analysis reveals a distinctly conservative nature: LLMs reliably extract terms on which humans consistently agree, but omit terms on which humans disagree. Our findings reveal the limitations of relying on a single gold standard, highlighting the need for annotator-aligned prompting and controllable precision–recall tuning.
