title: 3D-VITAL: Visibility-aware Identity Training from Artificial Liftings of 3D Reconstruction model for Cross-View Object Re-Identification
abstract: We address the Cross-View Object Re-Identification (ReID) task, aiming to match identities across drastically different viewpoints. We focus on Single-View Aerial-Ground ReID (SV AG-ReID), where models train on one viewpoint and must generalize to another at inference. To bridge this viewpoint gap, related work employs generative models to synthesize novel views from source images as additional training data. We leverage recent advances in large-scale single-view 3D mesh reconstruction to lift source images into textured meshes and to render them from new viewpoints. However, this pipeline produces unreliable data in two distinct ways. First, the reconstruction may fail and produce geometrically incorrect meshes, resulting in severe corruption in rendered novel views. Second, even when the geometry is correct, the rendered novel views contain hallucinated textures in regions not visible in the source image. The reconstructed mesh carries a per-pixel partition between regions visible from the source view and regions that the reconstruction model had to hallucinate, available as a deterministic byproduct of rendering. We introduce this per-pixel visibility map and exploit it in a two-stage design. Cross-View Consistency Filtering (CVCF) discards geometrically incorrect meshes by ensuring multi-view consistency between source and novel views over visible patches. Visibility-Aware Attention Supervision (VAAS) leverages the visibility map to guide the model's attention toward reliable regions of the rendered view during training. Combined, these two components enable our method, 3D-VITAL, to better leverage the synthetic signal from single-view 3D mesh reconstruction. 3D-VITAL sets a new state-of-the-art on three SV AG-ReID benchmarks. Code and data will be released at https://github.com/TurtleSmoke/3D-VITAL.

title: Tikhonov-Stabilized Bezier Representation Forecasting for Training-free Diffusion Acceleration
abstract: Diffusion models, particularly Diffusion Transformers, achieve strong image and video generation quality but remain expensive at inference time due to repeated denoiser evaluations. Feature caching offers a deployment-friendly acceleration strategy by reusing or predicting intermediate representations without retraining the generator or modifying the sampler. However, existing cache-then-forecast methods often rely on Taylor-style finite-difference extrapolation, which can become unstable over longer cache intervals, and typically predict local module outputs whose errors may accumulate through subsequent denoiser blocks. We propose \textbf{BeziCast}, a training-free diffusion acceleration framework that forecasts output-proximal denoising representations using low-order B'ezier trajectories. BeziCast estimates B'ezier control points via Tikhonov-stabilized fitting, providing a smooth, capacity-controlled temporal parameterization that avoids explicit high-order derivative estimation and decouples trajectory capacity from cache-query density. To moderate aggressive extrapolation, we further derive equivalent forecasting weights and introduce a convex-hull-inspired guardrail that detects high-risk predictions and softly pulls them toward a conservative simplex-projected estimate. Extensive evaluations across advanced image and video diffusion models demonstrate the effectiveness of BeziCast. In particular, BeziCast accelerates FLUX.1 by up to (4.79\times) and HunyuanVideo by up to (4.11\times), while preserving substantially better generation quality than competing acceleration baselines.

title: Improving LLM Reliability Through Adaptive Detection
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) transition from isolated research prototypes into integrated production systems, they encounter a critical safety-utility trade-off. Conventional safety mechanisms typically force a binary operational choice: either deploy strict, static guardrails that prevent harmful outputs but induce severe over-refusal of benign queries, or utilize relaxed controls that preserve usability at the cost of exposing users to unsafe generation. Furthermore, approaches that rely on scalar confidence signals lack contextual awareness, and monolithic API guardrails often introduce prohibitive latency bottlenecks. To resolve this socio-technical dilemma, we propose a multi-dimensional Adaptive Abstention System that models LLM refusal as a context-sensitive, dynamic decision-making process. Grounded in a Lagrangian risk minimization framework, our architecture automatically calibrates its abstention thresholds in real-time based on domain sensitivity and historical user trust. The system evaluates prompt risk across five orthogonal dimensions: safety, predictive confidence, knowledge boundaries, contextual appropriateness, and conversational repetition. To ensure low-latency inference, these detectors are arranged in a 4-level cost-sensitive cascade. Detector weights were optimized via Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Bayesian optimization, shifting reliance from raw perplexity to distribution entropy and epistemic hedging. Extensive empirical evaluation across 10,000+ benchmark interactions (including AdvBench, ToxiGen, and XSTest) demonstrates that the proposed architecture achieves a Macro-F1 of 0.957 while reducing benign false-positive refusals by up to 80\% in specialized domains. Operational stress testing confirms production viability, successfully sustaining 895 requests per second with a 99th-percentile (P99) latency of 110 ms and an expected fast-path execution time of 4.3 ms on consumer-grade hardware.

title: The Model Is in the Wrong Seat
abstract: Agents today start from one premise: take the person in the control seat and put a model there instead. That seat was shaped around a person, and a model doesn't fit it. The fix isn't a better model or a better harness. It's a different starting point. This essay introduces AI-Oriented Programming and its two principles: assume the model can be wrong at any time without telling you, and assume the system will live in a world of agents. Chapter 0 of the AI-Oriented Programming series, first published on LinkedIn and X on October 12, 2026.

title: An Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation Agent for UAV Situation Awareness Report Generation
abstract: Accurate and timely UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle) situation awareness is essential for early warning and operational decision-making in low-altitude security, yet the manual analysis of large-scale heterogeneous data is resource-intensive and introduces delays. This study proposes IRAG-UAVSA (Improved Retrieval-Augmented Generation—Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Situation Awareness) Agent, an autonomous situation-awareness report-generation framework based on an improved retrieval-augmented generation architecture. The framework integrates real-time UAV descriptors, including platform type, intent, and threat level, with four task-specific hierarchical knowledge bases. A dual-loop pipeline combines evidence-template-guided hybrid retrieval and cross-encoder reranking with high-level LLM (Large Language Model) reflection, structured evidence filling, rule-based validation, and threshold-triggered iterative retry. A three-level evaluation framework was designed, comprising process-level RAG metrics, automatic natural language evaluation, and human–LLM collaborative scoring. Across 49 domain-screened test inputs, IRAG-UAVSA Agent achieved 93.0% knowledge coverage, 4.1% hallucination, and 91.7% logical consistency, while also obtaining the best SummaC (0.67) and VeriScore (0.83) results among the evaluated baselines. The results indicate that iterative retrieval with explicit evidence constraints can substantially improve the factual grounding, traceability, and practical utility of LLM-generated UAV situation-awareness reports.

title: Fourteen reusable building blocks (RBBs) for representing decision-making in agent-based models: a compilation on AGENTBLOCKS providing practical guidance and ways forward
abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used to study socio–environmental systems. By integrating environmental modelling with behavioural theories, they enable to analyse how decision-making processes shape environmental outcomes. To speed up model development and enable cumulative theorising, it has been proposed to modularise components relevant across applications as reusable building blocks (RBBs). This paper describes an example of adopting the idea in practice using AGENTBLOCKS, a new open access platform for publishing RBBs. We present the first coordinated interdisciplinary effort of eleven modelling groups to identify, extract, review, and publish 14 decision-making RBBs from existing ABMs using AGENTBLOCKS. From this compilation, we extracted a decision tree to identify and scope reusable model components. Using a mixed-methods approach combining RBB criteria assessment, thematic coding of editorial feedback, and contributor surveys, we suggest empirically informed practices and next steps to lower the barrier for reusable coding practices in socio–environmental applications.

title: Global advances in Generative AI for renewable energy and implications for sustainable energy transitions in Africa
abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being investigated for renewable-energy forecasting, optimisation, predictive maintenance, synthetic-data generation, and infrastructure planning. This study reviews global advances and critically assesses their implications for Africa's sustainable energy transition. It aims to: (i) map GenAI applications in renewable-energy systems; (ii) distinguish demonstrated results from proposed African opportunities; (iii) evaluate evidence quality, transferability, and deployment feasibility; and (iv) identify context-specific research and policy priorities. A systematic review was reported using PRISMA 2020, with the PRALSMA AI-assisted workflow used to support, but not replace, researcher-led screening and synthesis. OpenAlex records published from 2020 to May 2026 were screened, yielding 75 included studies. Manual analysis was triangulated with ChatGPT Project and NotebookLM, and findings were weighted by methodological quality, evidence maturity, and relevance to African data, grid, infrastructure, institutional, and cost conditions. The corpus remains geographically imbalanced: five of the 75 included studies report an African institutional affiliation (Morocco, Nigeria, and South Africa, with further co-affiliations in Tunisia and Gabon), and most quantitative outcomes still derive from non-African simulations, prototypes, or case studies. Consequently, reported error, cost, emission, and accuracy improvements are treated as source-specific rather than directly transferable African effects. Near-term priorities are controlled pilots of lightweight, explainable, offline-capable decision support and synthetic-data methods; compute-intensive diffusion, agentic, digital-twin, and imitation-learning applications require further validation. evidence.title: Global advances in Generative AI for renewable energy and implications for sustainable energy transitions in Africa
evidence.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is being investigated for renewable-energy forecasting, optimisation, predictive maintenance, synthetic-data generation, and infrastructure planning. This study reviews global advances and critically assesses their implications for Africa's sustainable energy transition. It aims to: (i) map GenAI applications in renewable-energy systems; (ii) distinguish demonstrated results from proposed African opportunities; (iii) evaluate evidence quality, transferability, and deployment feasibility; and (iv) identify context-specific research and policy priorities. A systematic review was reported using PRISMA 2020, with the PRALSMA AI-assisted workflow used to support, but not replace, researcher-led screening and synthesis. OpenAlex records published from 2020 to May 2026 were screened, yielding 75 included studies. Manual analysis was triangulated with ChatGPT Project and NotebookLM, and findings were weighted by methodological quality, evidence maturity, and relevance to African data, grid, infrastructure, institutional, and cost conditions. The corpus remains geographically imbalanced: five of the 75 included studies report an African institutional affiliation (Morocco, Nigeria, and South Africa, with further co-affiliations in Tunisia and Gabon), and most quantitative outcomes still derive from non-African simulations, prototypes, or case studies. Consequently, reported error, cost, emission, and accuracy improvements are treated as source-specific rather than directly transferable African effects. title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
abstract: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.

title: Ghost unitaries for loss-resilient photonic resource-state generation
abstract: Entangled few-photon states, such as Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, are central resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing. In many architectures, these states are generated probabilistically by first heralding single photons from biphoton sources and then interfering them in linear-optical circuits. In this work, we show that the entanglement structure of said biphoton sources can be directly exploited for noise-engineering to deliver higher quality resource states. Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, we introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations in which the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes rather than to the delivered resource modes. When the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss, this relocation converts direct amplitude damping of the output into false-positive heralding events that require both higher-pair emission and photon loss. In the low-squeezing regime, these events are parametrically suppressed, yielding higher-fidelity conditional resource states. We analyze this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, and a family of $n$-qubit GHZ states, as well as for single-qubit teleportation and type-I-fusion-based resource growth. Across these examples, we delineate finite parameter regimes in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations can be relatively lossy. We also prove that, in the setting considered here, the direct implementation of the $n$-GHZ family delivers identically damped outputs: equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping. This extends the known $n=2,3$ cases and provides a structural result of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.

title: DexNinja: Learning Robust Dexterous Cutting Policy with a Real-to-Sim-to-Real Data Engine
abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates or damages the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting is expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elasticity responses quickly compound. We propose \textsc{DexNinja}, a real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. \textsc{DexNinja} (i) reconstructs object instances from real captures, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters under category-level constraints, and (iii) produces augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate \textsc{DexNinja} on a dexterous food-slicing task and show that (1) with tens of real demonstrations and hundreds of augmented simulator data, the success rate could reach more than 60\%. (2) the augmented data consistently improves success rates when only using real data with more than 20\% via sim-to-real, and (3) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects with varying shapes and sizes.

title: DDVR-Net: Degradation-Aware Decoupling and Visibility-Guided Restoration for Historical Document Recognition
abstract: Historical document analysis is crucial for cultural heritage preservation and low-resource language digitization. However, real historical documents often suffer from severe degradation, such as ink erosion and structural damage, causing mixed-visibility character sequences. Conventional OCR systems struggle in such evidence-limited scenarios, while contextual language models may over-correct visually clear characters. To address these challenges, we propose DDVR-Net, a degradation-aware decoupling and visibility-guided restoration framework for historical document recognition. DDVR-Net decouples intrinsic glyph structures from physical corruption at the feature level and predicts local visibility to estimate character reliability. A contextual decoder is selectively activated through a visibility-guided gate, restoring degraded characters while preserving clear visual recognition. Furthermore, we construct a low-resource multilingual benchmark covering Tibetan, Mongolian, and Uyghur scripts with 187000 document pairs, combining large-scale synthetic data and progressive training with real-world annotations to reduce the synthetic-to-real gap. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DDVR-Net consistently outperforms existing methods across three languages and diverse reading orders, providing an effective framework and benchmark for low-resource historical document recognition. Code and Benchmark: https://github.com/Shajiu/DDVR-Net

title: Explaining Heterogeneous Treatment Effects with Causal Forests and the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition
abstract: The estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects is a central objective of causal inference. However, state-of-the-art algorithms to solve this task are based on machine learning principles, and thus behave as black boxes. Consequently, the identification of covariates driving heterogeneity remains a challenging and open problem. To address this limitation, we introduce CausalTreeHFD, an interpretable extension of causal forests, based on the Hoeffding functional decomposition adapted to tree ensembles. Our approach decomposes predictions of conditional average treatment effects (CATE) into contributions from individual covariates and pairwise interactions, providing a direct characterization of the factors driving treatment effect heterogeneity. We establish the consistency of CausalTreeHFD, which converges towards the Hoeffding decomposition of the underlying CATE function, under standard assumptions for the analysis of causal forests. Experiments on simulated and real datasets show that CausalTreeHFD accurately identifies relevant covariates and interactions, and precisely recovers their contributions to heterogeneous treatment effects.

title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Methods, Benefits, and Challenges for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly studied for tasks such as medical-image analysis, risk prediction, and clinical decision support. However, strong predictive performance does not by itself show why a model reached a particular conclusion or whether that conclusion is appropriate for a patient. This paper reviews explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods that can make healthcare predictions more understandable to clinicians and other stakeholders. A focused narrative review was conducted using foundational work on local explanations and Shapley-value-based feature attribution, a healthcare-focused review, and World Health Organization guidance on AI ethics. The paper compares model-specific and model-agnostic explanations, with particular attention to LIME, SHAP, and visual explanation methods. The review indicates that explanations can support error analysis, communication, and model auditing, but they should not be treated as proof that a prediction is correct, fair, or clinically safe. Explanation quality depends on data quality, model behaviour, the intended user, and the clinical context. The paper proposes a practical evaluation framework combining predictive performance, explanation fidelity, stability, clinical usefulness, fairness checks, and human oversight. It concludes that XAI should be integrated into the full lifecycle of clinical AI systems rather than added only after model development. Index Terms—Explainable AI, healthcare, clinical decision support, interpretability, SHAP, LIME.

title: AI for Solar Energy Systems
abstract: The rapid expansion of solar energy has accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve forecasting accuracy, photovoltaic performance, intelligent control, fault diagnosis, energy storage management, and smart grid operation. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, Digital Twins, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Edge AI, Federated Learning, and Generative AI have transformed solar energy systems into more adaptive and data-driven infrastructures. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model generalization, computational efficiency, cybersecurity, and explainability continue to limit large-scale deployment. An integrated perspective is presented by connecting AI applications across photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technologies, energy storage, and intelligent energy networks within a unified renewable energy ecosystem. Emerging research trends and future directions highlight the evolution toward AI-native energy systems that support efficient, resilient, and sustainable intelligent societies.

title: Structure-Preserving Reinforcement Learning for Language Models: Leveraging Geometry
abstract: We propose a geometric framework for structure-preserving reinforcement learning in the fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), grounded in Lie algebraic geometry. The approach systematically identifies geometric constraints in representation spaces by analyzing semantic transformations and detecting cases where embed- dings exhibit approximate Lie group structures. When such structure is present, we introduce reinforcement learning algorithms that respect these constraints through projection-based policy gradient updates. We provide theoretical guarantees of convergence and derive sample complexity bounds that depend on the intrinsic geomet- ric dimensionality rather than the full parameter space. The framework is particularly effective when language representations reveal coherent geometric patterns that encode semantic relations. Although empirical validation remains ongoing, this work establishes a principled foundation for integrating geometric priors into language model alignment, offering improved efficiency, stability, and interpretability from the perspectives of differential geometry and representation theory.

title: Strong Solvers, Leaky Tutors: Evaluating Answer Leakage in LLM Math Tutors
abstract: Educational digital libraries may grant large language model (LLM) tutors access to worked solutions, but access to repository content should not automatically authorize a model to reveal final answers. This study evaluates whether LLM tutors can leverage private solution context to generate pedagogical hints without disclosing final answers to students. Four models, two general instruction-following models and two math-specialized models, are evaluated across 5,000 aligned problem–message cases per condition, constructed from 500 MATH benchmark problems paired with ten fixed student prompts that ask for, or attempt to confirm, the final answer. Three prompting strategies are compared: a plain assistant prompt, a basic tutoring prompt, and a two-step method that generates a private solution before producing numbered hints. The basic tutoring prompt reduces detected answer leakage from 47.4% to 0.3% for GPT-4o-mini and from 30.2% to 1.0% for LLaMA-3.1, but produces no comparable improvement for Qwen2.5-Math or DeepSeek-Math. Under identical strict hint rules, adding private solution context has minimal effect on GPT but significantly improves tutoring compliance for LLaMA; Qwen produces the most accurate private solutions yet shows the highest leakage and solution-to-hint overlap. These results indicate that private solution access can support hint generation in some architectures but is not a reliable answer-withholding mechanism on its own. For educational digital libraries, access to solution content and authorization to disclose it should be treated as distinct access-control decisions.

title: Assessing the Performance of AI Models in Misinformation Detection Using Predefined Social Noise Constructs
abstract: Social media platforms generate vast volumes of user-generated content that often obscure meaningful discourse, a phenomenon conceptualized as social noise. While existing misinformation detection methods primarily focus on factual verification, they largely overlook the role of social noise in amplifying misinformation. This study assesses the performance of six text-based models and a graph neural network (GNN) in mitigating the effects of misinformation using predefined social noise constructs. The dataset consists of 500,000 tweets collected from the X platform using the Ukraine hashtag during the Russia-Ukraine conflict from March 2024 to March 2025. Advanced machine learning models achieve strong performance, with accuracies ranging from 79.94% to 97.17%. RoBERTa demonstrates the highest performance, with an accuracy of 97.17%, Cohen's kappa of 0.9660, MCC of 0.9660, and AUC of 0.9977. The GNN achieves an accuracy of 64.52% and an AUC of 0.899, demonstrating performance above random-chance classification by exploiting the relational structure between tweets. All text-based models achieve kappa values greater than 0.75, indicating substantial overall agreement. Explainable AI analysis using LIME reveals that 89.6% of predictive weight is attributed to contextual features rather than isolated keywords. The findings highlight that integrating social noise into AI pipelines enhances misinformation detection and supports more effective mitigation strategies in large-scale social media environments.

title: AutoMARS: Automatic and Scalable Multi-Agent Large Language Model Framework for Supply Chain Risk Assessment
abstract: We propose AutoMARS (Automatic Multi-Agent Risk Assessment), an agentic framework for automatic and scalable comparative risk assessment in supply chain networks. The framework enables end-to-end execution of analytical workflows by automatically planning tasks, coordinating specialized agents, invoking external analytical tools, and synthesizing domain-specific results into integrated risk evaluations. AutoMARS further supports scalable risk comparison across multiple locations by parallelizing independent analytical tasks. The framework adopts a multi-domain, multi-agent, and multi-tool architecture that integrates heterogeneous risk factors from socioeconomic, disaster, environmental, and transportation domains. Through coordinated agent interactions and tool integration, AutoMARS enables structured, systematic, and interpretable comparative analysis to support supply chain risk-aware location evaluation.

title: Spectral Costs of Multinomial and Residual Resampling in High-Dimensional Particle Ensembles: A Free-Probability Analysis
abstract: Resampling is the standard remedy against weight degeneracy in particle filters, yet its effect on the spectrum of the particle second-moment matrix is poorly understood. We study a single resampling step for a d-dimensional ensemble of N particles with d/N -> c. For any unbiased scheme, the resampled empirical second-moment matrix dominates its pre-resampling counterpart in conditional convex order, while the conditional mean is preserved; the excess second spectral moment equals the Frobenius energy of the resampling perturbation. For multinomial resampling, the empirical count law converges to the mixed-Poisson law determined by the limiting weight law. For residual resampling, the count law is determined by the joint limit of floor-fraction pairs: we classify all residual limits of weight sequences converging to delta_1 in law as a one-parameter family between the deterministic identity and the full multinomial count law. Each count law feeds a common covariance-side spectral map, yielding exact consequences: a closed-form zero-eigenvalue mass, a rank-and-spectral-gap transition with a universal lower edge benchmark, computable regular edges, unbounded right support, and scheme-specific second-moment costs. The effective sample size determines one bulk statistic but cannot determine the limiting spectrum. Pre-registered numerical experiments confirm the theory at every level.

For residual resampling, the count law is determined by the joint limit of floor-fraction pairs: we classify all residual limits of weight sequences converging to delta_1 in law as a one-parameter family between the deterministic identity and the full multinomial count law. Each count law feeds a common covariance-side spectral map, yielding exact consequences: a closed-form zero-eigenvalue mass, a rank-and-spectral-gap transition with a universal lower edge benchmark, computable regular edges, unbounded right support, and scheme-specific second-moment costs. The effective sample size determines one bulk statistic but cannot determine the limiting spectrum. Pre-registered numerical experiments confirm the theory at every level.

title: Pixels or Code? Benchmarking Instruction-Guided Visual Artifact Operation
abstract: Visual artifacts such as charts, technical diagrams, webpages, and document pages underpin scientific, commercial, and engineering workflows. Editing these artifacts requires direct modification, dependency-aware updates, preservation of unaffected content, and compliance with domain constraints. We define this capability as Visual Artifact Operation (VAO). Prior benchmarks test parts of this problem, including cascading updates in charts. We study direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation across visual domains and pixel, code, and agent paradigms under one image-only protocol. We introduce Visual Artifact Operation Bench (VAO-Bench), comprising 1,573 manually screened tasks across nine artifact categories and three difficulty levels. VAO-Bench uses executable artifacts and deterministic rendering to trace reference transformations and annotate direct edits, dependent updates, and preservation constraints. All systems receive the same source image and instruction; we evaluate pixel-space editors, code-generating multimodal systems, and tool-using agents on direct-edit accuracy, dependency-aware update, content preservation, domain validity, and visual quality. Experiments show that executable-code systems better support dependent updates, while pixel-space editors offer faster execution and strong visual quality. Explicitly stating dependencies improves both paradigms, identifying implicit-update inference as a central bottleneck. VAO-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for dependable visual artifact editing across generation paradigms.

title: Ontological Engineering and Semantic Topical Authority in Large Language Models: A Holistic Framework for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
abstract: This paper presents an end-to-end ontological engineering framework based on the Holistic Semantic SEO and Topical Authority principles formalized by Koray Tuğberk Gübür, adapted specifically for Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) and neural search retrieval in frontier Large Language Models (LLMs). We define the topological requirements for closed-loop topical authority graphs that eliminate internal semantic cannibalization, enforce Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) graph coherence, and maximize contextual retrieval probability in architectures such as Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, and Perplexity AI. Empirical validation across enterprise DFY services (POS1 SEO Agency) and vocational education platforms (Aprender21) demonstrates sustained organic commercial performance with $0 in paid advertising spend.

title: A Two-way Interactive Secure Communication Model for Electric Energy Metering Data
abstract: INTRODUCTION: As power market reforms deepen, traditional unidirectional protocols (e.g., IEC 102) fail to meet the secure, real-time, and bidirectional data exchange requirements of modern power grids, leaving systems vulnerable to eavesdropping and tampering.OBJECTIVES: To ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and reliability of power data transmission by overcoming the pattern leakage vulnerabilities of traditional encryption, while satisfying the strict real-time and high-frequency demands of large-scale power systems.METHODS: Two schemes are designed: a pure SM4 symmetric encryption scheme for high-frequency data, and an SM2-SM4 hybrid scheme for advanced authentication. To enhance security, a novel ECB-CBC hybrid encryption mode is introduced for SM4. RESULTS: The proposed ECB-CBC hybrid mode effectively eliminates plaintext redundancy. Its Shannon entropy stabilizes at ~7.99 bits/byte (nearly touching the 8.0 theoretical ideal, vastly improving upon standard ECB's ~3.5 bits/byte). It also achieves an optimal inter-block avalanche effect of ~64 bits per block. The SM2-SM4 hybrid scheme's encryption time is only 15%-20% higher than that of pure SM4. Across 1-16 thread tests, the throughput of both SM4-based schemes grows linearly, outperforming RSA and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) by several orders of magnitude.CONCLUSION: The proposed ECB-CBC hybrid architecture overcomes standard mode vulnerabilities and achieves the macro-level Strict Avalanche Criterion (SAC), significantly enhancing resistance to network attacks. Compared to traditional asymmetric and homomorphic encryption, the SM4 and SM2-SM4 schemes strike an optimal balance between robust security and computational efficiency for high-concurrency power system applications.

title: Fibonacci–Lucas Recurrence-Indexed Quaternionic Unitaries: Channel Convergence, Clifford Proximity, and Controlled Entanglement
abstract: We investigate the normalized operator geometry of the mixed Fibonacci–Lucas quaternion Qn = Fn + Lni + Fn+1j + Ln+1k. Standard quaternion representations associate this sequence with single-qubit unitary channels. We first establish a convergence theorem for quaternion sequences with two distinct real characteristic roots and a strictly dominant positive root. It gives an exact average gate infidelity to the limit and sharp projective-step asymptotics, including the degenerate constant-channel case. For the Fibonacci–Lucas assignment, orthogonal Binet coefficient vectors yield exact finite-index formulas with projective steps of order φ−2n and average gate infidelities of order φ−4n. Strict comparison of the five projective Clifford rotation classes proves that the limiting unitary has a unique nearest projective Clifford, the cyclic Pauli-axis permutation, with average gate fidelity 115+5/90≈0.884408. For the controlled family, product-input maximization gives concurrence 1−an2, while independent Haar averaging gives linear-entropy entangling power 21−an2/9. Both admit explicit algebraic limits. Reproducible matrix and high-precision scalar calculations verify these results. The analysis supplies exact convergence, finite-group, and entanglement benchmarks for a recurrence-indexed family without assuming Hamiltonian dynamics.

title: Can LLMs Reason Over Where and When? Benchmarking Spatiotemporal Synthesis in Crisis Response
abstract: Situational awareness during crises depends on synthesizing fragmented reports that vary across time, location, and source. Reliable crisis question answering must prioritize recent and nearby reports while reconciling updates that contradict earlier information. However, existing crisis datasets often provide insufficient evidence for systematically evaluating these capabilities. We audit evidence coverage across crisis-need queries and enrich under-covered cases with synthetic situational-awareness posts, constructing sequences of reports and updates that preserve spatiotemporal consistency. Using the enriched benchmark, we compare direct prompting, structured prompting, and ST-CrisisSynth, which applies query-dependent semantic, spatial, and temporal weights to re-rank evidence before generation. Human evaluation shows that ST-CrisisSynth achieves the highest correct-response rate (70.0%), improving by 3.3 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These findings suggest that selecting and organizing spatiotemporal evidence before generation supports more reliable crisis information synthesis.

title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Blind Quantum Machine Learning
abstract: Can quantum advantages in computational efficiency coexist with quantum advantages in privacy? In this paper, we construct and use MasonQ, a universal brickwork transpiler, to answer this question with a resounding yes. We approach this question by bridging two seemingly disparate paradigms: universal blind quantum computation (UBQC), based on measurement-based quantum computation, and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms such as the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm and quantum recommendation systems. We provide new upper bounds on the depth of UBQC brickwork graphs, establishing that $D = \mathcal{O}(ωn)$, where $ω$ is the circuit width and $n$ its computational gate complexity. This is enabled by our newly developed transpiler MasonQ, which maps arbitrary quantum circuits to computational brickwork graph states. Given an optimal Qiskit circuit as input, we prove optimality (up to logarithmic corrections) of the MasonQ transpiler in terms of asymptotic scaling of the total brickwork graph width and depth after decomposition into bricks, enabling systematic cost analyses of blind implementations in near-term experiments and asymptotic regimes. Leveraging MasonQ, we derive depth bounds for several representative blind quantum machine learning (B-QML) algorithms, including the quantum Fourier transform, the HHL algorithm, recommendation systems, and quantum transformers. Lastly, we analyze concrete resource estimates for near-term demonstrations of blind quantum machine learning. We propose a minimal B-QML implementation requiring only a $12$ qubit quantum server. To the best of our knowledge, MasonQ is the first functional and optimal universal circuit-to-brickwork-graph transpiler to implement the full brickwork transpilation process from first principles.

title: Learning to Design Convex Relaxations for Nonconvex Optimization
abstract: Convex relaxations make nonconvex optimization tractable by replacing hard nonconvex problems with convex surrogates that give valid bounds. Yet their design is still largely manual: a human expert must decide where to relax, which relaxation to use, and how much formulation growth is worth paying. We show that this design process can be learned. The method proposed in this paper, AutoConvexRelax, represents the symbolic formulation of a nonconvex problem as a tripartite graph linking variables, symbolic terms, and their objective or constraint positions. It then learns a policy that composes symbolic rewrites into problem-specific relaxation trajectories as the formulation evolves. We prove that finite action sequences generated by the learned policy preserve relaxation validity under explicit domain, occurrence-context, and representation-consistency conditions. We further establish computable error bounds for mixed relaxations and sufficient conditions for feasible recovery and global-optimality certification. As a first instantiation, we apply the method to nonconvex quadratic problems and fractional problems. On 241 benchmark quadratic instances, the learned policy strengthens McCormick lower bounds by 13.52%. Its mean lower bound is 3.70% below strengthened semidefinite relaxations on the normalized comparison metric, while it uses substantially smaller formulations. The learned policy retains this trade-off on fractional instances and reaches near-semidefinite bounds on beamforming and sensor-network localization instances. These results suggest that convex relaxation design can move from a fixed handcrafted choice to an automated learning process that adapts to problem structures. Code is available at https://github.com/auto4opt/AutoConvexRelax.

title: EvoSpatial: Experience-Driven Skill and Tool Evolution for Spatial Reasoning Agents
abstract: Spatial reasoning agents can inspect tool outputs and repair errors, but reusing these lessons requires preserving both the computation and the conditions that make it valid. We introduce EvoSpatial, a framework that learns from execution experience by updating a library of linked skills and tools. Skills describe procedures, geometric assumptions, and verification steps; tools implement the operations those procedures require. When solving a task, the agent retrieves relevant skills and synthesizes reusable computational functions if existing tools are insufficient. After each task, execution feedback and evidence checks guide skill revision and tool consolidation, without ground-truth answers or benchmark scores. Across 20 benchmarks, EvoSpatial averages 63.9, 4.0 percentage points above the average reported by SpatialClaw. The evolved library also improves held-out and cross-benchmark performance when updates are disabled, and trajectories generated with evolved skills improve supervised fine-tuning, even without external skills at evaluation. Keeping checked procedures on record, together with the tools that support them, lets an agent carry spatial reasoning experience from one task to the next.

title: Efficient agentic AI: A framework for adaptive test-time scaling, resource-aware evaluation and adaptive reasoning
abstract: Agentic AI systems leverage large reasoning models that are increasingly using longer chains of thought, parallel sampling, search, or verifier-guided refinement at test time to make use of additional compute. This additional compute is typically wasted: agents "overthink" simple sub-tasks, redo tool calls for no particular reason, and allow context to accumulate over time through long tasks. In this paper, we will study efficiency in agentic reasoning systems from six perspectives. First, a taxonomy of test-time scaling strategies for agentic workloads. Second, a multi-dimensional efficiency framework including compute, latency, tokens, cost, energy, memory and task success. Third, a conceptual description of the reasoning efficiency frontier, based on patterns of results reported in the reasoning-model literature, showing where more reasoning might be beneficial, where it ceases to be beneficial, and where it might be counterproductive. Fourth, a benchmarking approach that is not only proposed for single-turn inference but also for agentic workloads. Fifth, an Adaptive Test-time Scaling Controller with task difficulty and model uncertainty-constrained reasoning budgets. Sixth, a taxonomy of modes of failure of agentic pipelines, with examples. It is this paper's position that adaptive budgeting should realize a significant portion of the accuracy that is obtainable with maximal test-time scaling that could be obtained at a much higher compute expense. It's a conceptual finding, backed up in the frontier analysis performed in Section 5, and not a measured result. The paper additionally proposes that much of the wasted compute in agentic systems is likely to be attributable to more factors than just reasoning, such as retries, context growth and multi-agent coordination.

title: Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core: Universal Thermodynamic Homeostasis & Epistemic Multi-Anchoring
abstract: Conventional AI guardrail frameworks rely on extrinsic, post-generation text filters, regex wrappers, or trailing output classifiers. By evaluating generated text after latent state transitions have completed, extrinsic systems operate with severe diagnostic latency, introducing metastable strain and creating critical vulnerabilities to prompt injections, deceptive alignment, and reward hacking. This paper specifies the Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core—a substrate-agnostic, dual-head thermodynamic control framework for autoregressive language models. By evaluating residual stream activation kinematics in memory during prefill and decoding, the Sentinel Core constructs an invariant State Uncertainty Coordinate grounded in statistical mechanics and Landauer's Principle. The architecture partitions latent acceleration into tangential semantic velocity and orthogonal boundary shear , preserving model agentic agency via prefill-extracted context centroids while enforcing deterministic 0-token prefill eviction and 1–3 token decode vetoes Fused Top-K logit steering and a dual-tier containment architecture (userspace stream cancellation and kernel-level eBPF socket drops).

This paper specifies the Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core—a substrate-agnostic, dual-head thermodynamic control framework for autoregressive language models. By evaluating residual stream activation kinematics in memory during prefill and decoding, the Sentinel Core constructs an invariant State Uncertainty Coordinate grounded in statistical mechanics and Landauer's Principle. The architecture partitions latent acceleration into tangential semantic velocity and orthogonal boundary shear , preserving model agentic agency via prefill-extracted context centroids while enforcing deterministic 0-token prefill eviction and 1–3 token decode vetoes Fused Top-K logit steering and a dual-tier containment architecture (userspace stream cancellation and kernel-level eBPF socket drops).
